(وَكَذلِكَ نَجْزِي مَنْ أَسْرَفَ وَلَمْ يُؤْمِنْ بِآياتِ رَبِّهِ وَلَعَذابُ الْآخِرَةِ أَشَدُّ وَأَبْقى): وكذلك is an adjective of an omitted maṣdar; نجزي is an imperfect verb and its fāʿil is latent, its implied form being "we"; من is a relative noun, the mafʿūl bihi, and the clause أسرف is its ṣila (relative clause). ولم يؤمن is conjoined to أسرف, so it falls within the scope of the ṣila; بآيات is attached to يؤمن, and ربه is muḍāf ilayhi. ولعذاب: the wāw is circumstantial or a conjunction; the lām is of commencement (ibtidāʾ); عذاب is a mubtadaʾ, الآخرة is muḍāf ilayhi, أشد is the khabar, and أبقى is conjoined to أشد. (أَفَلَمْ يَهْدِ لَهُمْ كَمْ أَهْلَكْنا قَبْلَهُمْ مِنَ الْقُرُونِ يَمْشُونَ فِي مَساكِنِهِمْ): the hamza is interrogative and is prefixed to something omitted, onto which [what follows] is conjoined with the fāʾ; this has been set out many times before, and we repeat it now as a reminder. The implied sense is: "Were they heedless, so that it has not become clear to them?" The fāʿil of يهد is the maṣdar understood from أهلكنا, i.e. "Has not our destruction [of them] become clear to them?" It is also possible that the fāʿil of يهد is a pronoun referring to Allah the Exalted, i.e. "Has Allah not made it clear?", but the first is preferable, because يهدي means "becomes clear", so it is intransitive, and the fāʿil is the clause cast into a maṣdar, namely أهلكنا. The Basrans rejected a clause occurring as a fāʿil, while others allowed it. Al-Qaffāl said: He made the great number of generations He destroyed a clarification for them. Al-Naḥḥās said: This is a mistake, because كم is interrogative, so what precedes it cannot govern it. Al-Zajjāj said: The meaning is: "Has not the matter of Our destroying those whom We destroyed guided them?" and its reality points to guidance, so the fāʿil is the guidance. لهم is attached to يهد; كم is the predicative (khabariyya) kam, a fronted mafʿūl bihi of أهلكنا; من القرون is an adjective of the tamyīz (specification) of the predicative kam, i.e. "how many a generation among the generations", and what is meant is the nation. The clause يمشون في مساكنهم is a ḥāl of the object of أهلكنا or of the pronoun in لهم; في مساكنهم is attached to يمشون, and the pronoun refers to those destroyed (al-muhlakīn, with fatḥa on the lām). He means that Quraysh move about in the lands of ʿĀd and Thamūd and see with their own eyes the traces of their destruction, in which there is what calls to taking heed and admonition. Abū al-Ṭayyib [al-Mutanabbī] aimed at the heights of this meaning, as will come in the section on rhetoric. (إِنَّ فِي ذلِكَ لَآياتٍ لِأُولِي النُّهى): inna and its fronted khabar, the shifted lām (al-lām al-muzaḥlaqa), and آيات is its postponed noun; لأولي is an adjective of آيات, and النهى is muḍāf ilayhi; it is the plural of نهية, meaning intellect.
(وَلَوْلا كَلِمَةٌ سَبَقَتْ مِنْ رَبِّكَ لَكانَ لِزاماً وَأَجَلٌ مُسَمًّى): the wāw is resumptive; لولا is a particle of non-occurrence due to the existence [of something]; كلمة is a mubtadaʾ whose khabar is omitted; the clause سبقت من ربك is an adjective of كلمة, and من ربك is attached to سبقت. لكان: the lām occurs in the apodosis of لولا; كان is a defective past verb, its noun is a latent pronoun, its implied form being "it", referring to the destruction, and لزاما is its khabar. وأجل مسمى is conjoined to كلمة, i.e. "and were it not for an appointed term, the destruction would have been binding upon them." It is also permissible, as al-Zamakhsharī and Abū al-Baqāʾ hold, that it be conjoined to the latent pronoun in «كان», i.e. "the immediate destruction and an appointed term would have been binding upon them, as they were binding upon ʿĀd and Thamūd." It is remarkable that most commentators, such as al-Jalāl, al-Bayḍāwī and others, followed this view despite the strain in it, and said: the separation by the khabar stands in place of the tawkīd (emphasis), because the proper form of the conjoining would have been to emphasize the latent pronoun in كان with a detached pronoun, so that one would say "it (هو) [is] binding, and an appointed term". There is no need for all this strain; conjoining it to كلمة is easier and quicker in conveying the intended meaning. (فَاصْبِرْ عَلى ما يَقُولُونَ وَسَبِّحْ بِحَمْدِ رَبِّكَ قَبْلَ طُلُوعِ الشَّمْسِ وَقَبْلَ غُرُوبِها): the fāʾ is the faṣīḥa (the fāʾ of an implied condition), i.e. "if the matter is as stated, that the postponement of their punishment is not neglect but respite, and that it will befall them and come upon them, then be patient." اصبر is an imperative verb, its fāʿil is latent, its implied form being "you"; على ما is attached to اصبر, and the clause يقولون is the ṣila; سبح is conjoined to اصبر; بحمد ربك is in the position of accusative as a ḥāl, i.e. "while you are praising your Lord for having enabled you to glorify Him and helped you in it." What is meant by patience will come in the section on benefits. قبل is attached to سبح, and طلوع الشمس is muḍāf ilayhi [Translator's note: the source has «مضاف», evidently meaning muḍāf ilayhi]; وقبل غروبها is conjoined to قبل طلوع الشمس. (وَمِنْ آناءِ اللَّيْلِ فَسَبِّحْ وَأَطْرافَ النَّهارِ لَعَلَّكَ تَرْضى): the preposition and its genitive noun are attached to سبح; the fāʾ is also the faṣīḥa; سبح is an imperative verb, its fāʿil is latent, its implied form being "you"; أطراف النهار is accusative, conjoined to the position of «ومن آناء», which is accusative, and it may also be conjoined to قبل طلوع الشمس. لعل is a particle of hope that makes [its noun] accusative; the kāf is its noun, and the clause ترضى is its khabar. What نرضى [Translator's note: so in the source; the word is ترضى] is attached to is omitted, understood from the context, i.e. "with the reward you are given". The clause لعلك ترضى is a ḥāl of the fāʿil of سبح, i.e. "pray, while hoping that Allah the Exalted will satisfy you with the reward He gives you." (وَلا تَمُدَّنَّ عَيْنَيْكَ إِلى ما مَتَّعْنا بِهِ أَزْواجاً مِنْهُمْ زَهْرَةَ الْحَياةِ الدُّنْيا لِنَفْتِنَهُمْ فِيهِ): the wāw is a conjunction; لا is prohibitive; تمدن is an imperfect verb, indeclinable (mabnī) on the fatḥa because it is attached to the nūn of emphasis, and it is in the position of jussive by لا; its fāʿil is a latent pronoun, its implied form being "you"; عينيك is the mafʿūl bihi; إلى ما is attached to تمدن, and the clause متعنا is the ṣila; به is attached to متعنا, and the hāʾ is the returning pronoun. أزواجا is the object of متعنا, i.e. "categories of them", and منهم is an adjective. It may also be parsed as accusative as a ḥāl of the pronoun hāʾ, in which case منهم is attached to متعنا. As for زهرة الحياة الدنيا, the grammarians went to great lengths in parsing it and brought the ways of its accusative to nine. We have sifted them and found them all acceptable, so we present them as they stated them in order to arrive at the preference:
1- That it is a second object, if we parse أزواجا as the first object, because the meaning of متعنا is "We gave".
2- That it is accusative as a ḥāl of the relative ما.
3- That it is accusative as a badal (substitute) of أزواجا, by way of hyperbole, as though they were the very blossom itself.
4- That it is accusative by an implied verb indicated by متّعنا, its implied form being "We made for them a blossom".
5- That it is accusative by way of censure (dhamm), i.e. "I censure the blossom of the life of this world".
6- That it is accusative by way of specification (ikhtiṣāṣ).
7- That it is accusative as a badal of the position of «به».
8- That it is accusative as a ḥāl of the pronoun in «به».
9- That it is accusative as a tamyīz of «ما» or of the hāʾ in «به».
From sifting these views and having regard to simplicity, it becomes clear that the accusative of زهرة is best taken as accusative by way of censure, or as an object on the basis that متعنا includes the meaning of أعطينا ("We gave"); al-Zamakhsharī and others began with these two.
لنفتنهم: the lām is of causation (taʿlīl); نفتنهم is an imperfect verb made accusative by an implied أن after the lām of causation; the preposition and its genitive noun are attached to متعناهم; the hāʾ is the mafʿūl bihi, and فيه is attached to نفتنهم. (وَرِزْقُ رَبِّكَ خَيْرٌ وَأَبْقى): the wāw is of the ḥāl; رزق ربك is a mubtadaʾ, خير is the khabar, and أبقى is conjoined to خير. (وَأْمُرْ أَهْلَكَ بِالصَّلاةِ وَاصْطَبِرْ عَلَيْها لا نَسْئَلُكَ رِزْقاً) وأمر: the wāw is resumptive or a conjunction; أمر is an imperative verb, its fāʿil is latent, its implied form being "you"; أهلك is the mafʿūl bihi, and بالصلاة is attached to the imperative verb; اصطبر is an imperative verb, its fāʿil is latent, its implied form being "you", and عليها is attached to اصطبر. The clause لا نسألك is resumptive; نسألك is an imperfect verb, a latent fāʿil and a mafʿūl bihi, and رزقا is a second mafʿūl bihi. (نَحْنُ نَرْزُقُكَ وَالْعاقِبَةُ لِلتَّقْوى): نحن is a mubtadaʾ and the clause نرزقك is the khabar; العاقبة is a mubtadaʾ and للتقوى is the khabar; these two clauses are also resumptive. (وَقالُوا لَوْلا يَأْتِينا بِآيَةٍ مِنْ رَبِّهِ أَوَلَمْ تَأْتِهِمْ بَيِّنَةُ ما فِي الصُّحُفِ الْأُولى): لولا is a particle of urging (taḥḍīḍ), i.e. "why not"; يأتينا is a verb, a latent fāʿil and a mafʿūl bihi; بآية is attached to يأتينا, and من ربه is attached to an omitted adjective of آية. They made this demand following their well-known way and their habit of obstinacy and stubbornness. أولم: the hamza is for the interrogative of denial, and the wāw is a conjunction onto something implied that the context requires, the implied sense being: "Have not clear proofs come to them in succession, and has there not come to them, in a special way, the clear proof of what is in the former scriptures?" بينة is the fāʿil of تأتهم; ما is a relative noun to which بينة is muḍāf; في الصحف is attached to an omitted ṣila of the relative noun, and الأولى is an adjective of الصحف. In it there is what suffices the fair-minded; as for the arrogant, obstinate one, how far it is that anything should convince him! (وَلَوْ أَنَّا أَهْلَكْناهُمْ بِعَذابٍ مِنْ قَبْلِهِ لَقالُوا رَبَّنا لَوْلا أَرْسَلْتَ إِلَيْنا رَسُولًا): the parsing of a construction like this has preceded, i.e. "if Our destruction [of them] had taken place"; so أنّا and what follows it is the fāʿil of an omitted verb, and the clause is resumptive, brought to reinforce what has been established about their obstinacy, arrogance and disputation. بعذاب is attached to أهلكناهم, and من قبله is an adjective of عذاب. لقالوا is the apodosis of لو, and the clause has no grammatical position. ربنا is a vocative muḍāf from which the vocative particle has been omitted; لولا is a particle of urging; أرسلت is a verb and its fāʿil; إلينا is attached to أرسلت, and رسولا is the mafʿūl bihi; the clause is the object of speech (maqūl al-qawl). (فَنَتَّبِعَ آياتِكَ مِنْ قَبْلِ أَنْ نَذِلَّ وَنَخْزى) فنتبع: the fāʾ is causal, and تنبع [Translator's note: so in the source, a misprint for نتبع] is accusative by an implied أن in the reply to the urging; the fāʿil is latent, its implied form being "we"; آياتك is the mafʿūl bihi, accusative with the kasra because it is a sound feminine plural; من قبل is attached to نتبع; أن and what follows it are interpreted as a maṣdar (interpreted maṣdar) to which قبل is muḍāf; نخزى is conjoined to نذل. (قُلْ كُلٌّ مُتَرَبِّصٌ فَتَرَبَّصُوا فَسَتَعْلَمُونَ مَنْ أَصْحابُ الصِّراطِ السَّوِيِّ وَمَنِ اهْتَدى): كل is a mubtadaʾ; beginning with it is permissible because of the meaning of generality in it; متربص is the khabar, and the clause is the object of speech. The fāʾ is the faṣīḥa, and تربصوا is an imperative verb. فستعلمون: the fāʾ is resumptive; the sīn is a particle of the future; تعلمون is an imperfect verb, nominative by the retention of the nūn, and the wāw is the fāʿil. من is an interrogative noun, a mubtadaʾ; أصحاب الصراط السوي is the khabar; ومن اهتدى is conjoined to من أصحاب; and the clause من أصحاب is the object of تعلمون, which is suspended (muʿallaq) from governing. It is also possible that من is a relative noun, the object of تعلمون, and أصحاب الصراط the khabar of an omitted mubtadaʾ, i.e. "they are the companions".

* Rhetoric:
1- Synecdoche (al-majāz al-mursal): He mentioned the generations (القرون) and meant the nations that live through them. Taking heed from the traces of nations that have perished and of generations gone by has been a source of inspiration for poets' imaginations, especially in elegy. The most brilliant of those who rose in imagination to this meaning are Abū al-Ṭayyib al-Mutanabbī and al-Buḥturī, so we confine ourselves to them, and we shall cite selected verses from two odes of theirs.
ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Muʿtazz, the Abbasid poet-caliph, said: "Had al-Buḥturī nothing but his ode on the Īwān of Khusraw (Kisrā) and his ode describing the pool of al-Mutawakkil, he would still be the greatest of poets." After he had grown weary of life in Baghdad following the killing of al-Mutawakkil ʿalā Allāh, al-Buḥturī visited al-Madāʾin, a city in which the Īwān of Khusraw stands. He described the Īwān with unique brilliance, made all the more splendid by the fact that, among the Arab poets, he was the first to describe the ancient, enduring monuments, draw inspiration from them and pour his own spirit into them. These are selections from it:
صنت نفسي عما يدنّس نفسي ... وترفعت عن جدا كلّ جبس
(I guarded my soul from what would sully it, and rose above the gifts of every base man.)
وتماسكت حيث زعزعني الده ... ر التماسا منه لتعسي ونكسي
(I held firm when Time shook me, seeking my ruin and my downfall.)
حضرت رحلي الهموم فوجه ... ت إلى أبيض المدائن عنسي
(Cares came to my camp, so I turned my camel toward the White Palace of al-Madāʾin.)
ذكرتنيهم الخطوب التوالي ... ولقد تذكر الخطوب وتنسي
(Successive calamities reminded me of them; calamities both remind and make forget.)
حلل لم تكن كأطلال سعدى ... في فقار من البسابس ملس
(Dwellings unlike the ruins of Suʿdā in smooth, barren wastes.)
فكأن الجرماز من عدم الأن ... س وإخلاله بنية رمس
(As if al-Jirmāz, for lack of company and its decay, were the structure of a tomb.)
لو تراه علمت أن الليالي ... جعلت فيه مأتما بعد عرس فإذا ما رأيت صورة انطا ... كية ارتعت بين روم
وفرس والمنايا مواثل وانوشر ... ... ... وان يزجي الصفوف تحت ال
درفس في اخضرار من اللباس على أص ... فر يختال في صبيغة
ورس عمرت للسرور دهرا فصارت ... للتعزي رباعهم وال
تأسي فلها ان أعينها بدموع ... موفقات على الصبابة حبس
(Were you to see it, you would know that the nights have made in it a funeral after a wedding. When you see the picture of Antioch [in the fresco], you take fright between Byzantines and Persians, with death standing present, and Anūshirwān driving the ranks under the banner, in green garments upon a yellow [horse], strutting in saffron-dyed dress. Their abodes were built for joy for an age, then became places of consolation and grief; it is fitting that I help them with tears devoted to longing.) [Translator's note: the verse divisions in the source are garbled in this passage; the Arabic is reproduced as printed.]
There is no room to cite the ode in full, for it is a living, expressive specimen of our Arabic literature, nor is there room to study it, so we confine ourselves to a few brief observations on it:
1- When you read the sīniyya (the ode rhyming in sīn), you feel the splendour of its music, arising from the lightness and beauty of the metre (al-khafīf) [Translator's note: the source has «الجر», evidently for «البحر», the metre], its harmony with the emotions, meanings and words, the whispered (mahmūs) rhyme letter, namely the sīn, and the repetition of whispered letters such as sīn, ṣād and tāʾ.
2- You feel the poet's being moved by grandeur when he begins to describe the Īwān, and then before long he grieves and sorrows when you read that the nights have made in it a funeral after a wedding. This psychological correspondence between what the poet describes and [the one who] describes is a purely artistic merit.
3- You feel that the poet admires everything great in the world, even if it is not of his own people; so we see him here admiring the Persians, weeping for them with the truest weeping and elegizing them with the most ardent elegy. Thus art rises until it turns into pure humanity.
4- Finally, you marvel that the poet opens up in Arabic literature a new art which no one before him had entered, namely elegy for vanished kingdoms and remaining monuments; no one pointed to it before the Quran, where Allah the Exalted says: «أَفَلَمْ يَهْدِ لَهُمْ كَمْ أَهْلَكْنا قَبْلَهُمْ مِنَ الْقُرُونِ يَمْشُونَ فِي مَساكِنِهِمْ إِنَّ فِي ذلِكَ لَآياتٍ لِأُولِي النُّهى».
We move on to the ʿayniyya (ode rhyming in ʿayn) of Abū al-Ṭayyib al-Mutanabbī, the ode in which he elegized Abū Shujāʿ Fātik, and in which he spoke of man's feeling before the traces left behind by their owners. From it he said:
إني لأجبن عن فراق أحبتي ... وتحسّ نفسي بالحمام فأشجع
(I am cowardly at parting from my loved ones, yet my soul senses death and I grow brave.)
ويزيدني غضب الأعادي قسوة ... ويلمّ بي عتب الصديق فأجزع
(The anger of enemies only increases my hardness, but a friend's reproach touches me and I am distressed.)
تصفو الحياة لجاهل أو غافل ... عما مضى فيها وما يتوقع
(Life is clear only for one ignorant or heedless of what has passed in it and what is expected.)
ولمن يغالط في الحقائق نفسه ... ويسومها طلب المحال فتطمع
(And for one who deceives himself about realities and charges his soul with seeking the impossible, so it covets.)
أين الذي الهرمان من بنيانه ... ما قومه ما يومه؟ ما المصرع تتخلّف الآثار عن أصحابها ... حينا ويدركها الفناء فتتبع
(Where is he whose building the two Pyramids are? Who were his people, what was his day, what his end? Monuments outlast their owners for a while, then annihilation overtakes them and they follow.)
It appears that Abū al-Ṭayyib loved the commander Fātik Abū Shujāʿ with a sincere love founded on admiration, for he elegized him with two odes which he made a means of expressing the cares and trials in his own soul; through them you see some philosophical reflections. As you see, he holds that life is clear only for the ignorant or the heedless, while the brave and proud man is seldom missed by its arrows. And here we see dark, gloomy meanings in his soul, to the point that he almost throws down his weapons before the misfortunes of time, were it not for a remnant of strength to which he holds fast:
المجد أخسر والمكارم صفقة ... من أن يعيش لها الهمام الأروع
(Glory and noble deeds are too losing a bargain for the bold, magnificent man to live for them.)
والناس أنزل في مكانك منزلا ... من أن تعايشهم وقدرك أرفع
(And people are of too low a station, in your eyes, for you to live among them when your rank is higher.)
2- In His saying «أَفَلَمْ يَهْدِ لَهُمْ ...» (the verse) there is the device of correspondence (al-munāsaba). It is of two kinds, conceptual and verbal. The conceptual kind is that the speaker begins with a meaning and then completes his speech with what corresponds to it in meaning, not in wording. [In the verse of al-Sajda that resembles this one,] the admonition of the verse is something heard, so He closed it with the most fitting conceptual correspondence by saying «أَفَلا يَسْمَعُونَ» [Translator's note: the source does not say so explicitly, but the closing «أَفَلا يَسْمَعُونَ» belongs to the parallel verse al-Sajda 32:26, not to Ṭā Hā 20:128]. And in the verse whose admonition is something seen, namely the verse of al-Sajda, He said: «أَوَلَمْ يَرَوْا أَنَّا نَسُوقُ الْماءَ إِلَى الْأَرْضِ الْجُرُزِ فَنُخْرِجُ بِهِ زَرْعاً تَأْكُلُ مِنْهُ أَنْعامُهُمْ وَأَنْفُسُهُمْ أَفَلا يُبْصِرُونَ», closing it with His saying:
«أَفَلا يُبْصِرُونَ», because that is something made clear by seeing; and there is no correspondence beyond this correspondence. Among the fine examples of it in poetry is the saying of al-Qāḍī al-Fāḍil:
وبدر بأفلاك الخواطر طالع ... وغصن بريحان الغدار وريق لئن بت في بحر من الفكر سابحا ... فإنسان عيني في الدموع غريق
(A full moon rising in the orbits of thoughts, and a bough leafy with the sweet basil of the cheek-down: if I spent the night swimming in a sea of thought, the pupil of my eye is drowned in tears.)
The correspondence in the first hemistich is among the full moon, the orbits and the rising; in the second hemistich between the bough, the basil and "leafy"; in the third between the sea and "swimming"; and in the fourth among the pupil of the eye (lit. "the man of the eye"), the tears and "drowned". So in every hemistich of the two verses there are numerous correspondences. As for verbal correspondence, it is of a lower rank than the conceptual one: it is bringing words of equal measure. It too is of two kinds, complete and incomplete. In the complete kind the words, besides being of equal measure, are rhymed; the incomplete kind is of equal measure but unrhymed. Among the examples of the complete kind from the Mighty Quran is the saying of the Exalted: «ن وَالْقَلَمِ وَما يَسْطُرُونَ، ما أَنْتَ بِنِعْمَةِ رَبِّكَ بِمَجْنُونٍ وَإِنَّ لَكَ لَأَجْراً غَيْرَ مَمْنُونٍ», and from poetry the saying of Ibn Hāniʾ al-Andalusī:
وعوابس وقوابس وفوارس ... وكوانس وأوانس وعقائل
(Frowning [steeds], fire-kindlers and horsemen, and secluded, gentle and noble maidens.)
Of the incomplete kind is the saying of Ibn Khalūf al-Maghribī:
كالورد خدا والغزالة بهجة ... والغصن قدا والغزال مقلدا
(Like the rose in cheek, the sun in radiance, the bough in stature and the gazelle in neck.)
The complete and incomplete kinds are combined in the saying of Abū Tammām:
مها الوحش إلا أن هاتا أوانس قنا الحظ إلا أن تلك ذوابل
(Wild oryx, except that these are tame; lances of al-Khaṭṭ, except that those are withered.) [Translator's note: the source prints «الحظ»; the well-known toponym is «الخط».]
Between قنا and مها there is complete verbal correspondence, and between الوحش and الحظ, and أوانس and ذوابل, there is incomplete correspondence.

* Benefits:
Abrogation (naskh) in the Quran:
In the saying of the Exalted «فَاصْبِرْ عَلى ما يَقُولُونَ» there is an important discussion worthy of reflection: most commentators have been accustomed to saying that this verse is abrogated by the verse of fighting. The correct view is that it is not abrogated; rather it is a command to praiseworthy patience in every circumstance, which is not being agitated and not being overcome by anxiety at what they say and at the harm that issues from them. There is in it no indication or hint at refraining from fighting, such that the command to fight could abrogate it.
The subject of abrogation in the Noble Quran is among the thorny, difficult subjects, and the disagreement over it is great. What is known in this area from an inductive survey of the speech of the Companions and the Successors is that they used "naskh" in the sense of the lexical meaning, which is the removal of one thing by another, not in the sense of the technical term of the legal theorists (uṣūliyyūn). For them, naskh meant the removal of some of the attributes of a verse by another verse: either by the expiry of the period of acting upon it, or by turning the speech from the immediately apparent meaning to a non-apparent one, or by showing that a certain restriction is incidental, or by specifying a general statement, or by showing the difference between what is explicitly stated and what was apparently analogized to it, or by removing a custom of the Jāhiliyya or a previous law. So the scope of naskh widened for them, the intellect roamed much there, and the circle of disagreement widened.
As for what is abrogated in the terminology of the later scholars, it is very little. Shaykh Jalāl al-Dīn al-Suyūṭī, in al-Itqān, mentioned in an extended treatment, as is fitting, some of what the scholars mentioned, and then established the abrogated verses on which the later scholars hold their view, following the imam, the ḥāfiẓ, the judge Abū Bakr Muḥammad ibn ʿAbd Allāh Ibn al-ʿArabī al-Maʿāfirī al-Andalusī; according to him there are close to twenty verses. In the modern era came Shaykh and Imam Muḥammad ʿAbduh, who denied abrogation in the Quran and said that everything they claimed to be abrogated can be interpreted, as you have seen in the saying of the Exalted «فَاصْبِرْ عَلى ما يَقُولُونَ». This is evident in this verse, and it overturns the old claim that the abrogated verses number about five hundred, a claim whose falsity is self-evident.

dervis-irab:83-86.t:
* Vocabulary:
(عَلى أَثَرِي): al-athar is the remainder of a thing; the plural is āthār and uthūr; [it also means] a report. «خرج في أثره وإثره»: he went out after him. ائتثره and تأثّره: he followed his track. Al-athar is also the damask grain of a sword, and it is also pronounced with kasra [al-ithr], like al-athīr; the plural is uthūr.
(السَّامِرِيُّ): In al-Qāmūs: the one who worshipped the calf; he was a non-Arab boor from Kirmān, or a great man of the Children of Israel. He is attributed to a tribe of the Children of Israel called al-Sāmira, an attribution to a district in Palestine. He said in al-Munjid: they are a people «who differ from the Jews on essential religious points, among them that of the books of revelation they acknowledge only the five books of Moses known as the Torah, and that they hold the duty of worship to be not in Jerusalem but on Mount Gerizim, south of Shechem». And he said in al-Khāzin: «His name was Mūsā ibn Ẓafar».

* I'rab:
(وَما أَعْجَلَكَ عَنْ قَوْمِكَ يا مُوسى): The wāw conjoins to something omitted which is understood from the context, the implied form being: "So Moses went to attend the appointed time with particular people", namely the seventy whom Moses chose from among his people to go with him to Mount al-Ṭūr to receive the Torah. He hastened ahead of them out of longing for the speech of his Lord and for the fulfilment of what he had been promised, based on his own judgement, and left them behind him; so the Exalted said to him: «وما أعجلك». More about this question will come in the section on Rhetoric. ما is an interrogative noun, a mubtadaʾ (subject); أعجل is a past verb with a latent (mustatir) fāʿil (agent), its implied form being "it", referring to ما; the kāf is the mafʿūl bihi (direct object); the clause is the khabar (predicate) of ما; عن قومك is a preposition and its genitive noun attached to (mutaʿalliq) أعجلك.
(قالَ هُمْ أُولاءِ عَلى أَثَرِي وَعَجِلْتُ إِلَيْكَ رَبِّ لِتَرْضى): هم is a mubtadaʾ and أولاء is the khabar; على أثري is a second khabar or a ḥāl (circumstantial); عجلت is a verb and its fāʿil, and the wāw is circumstantial with قد implied, or a conjunction; إليك is attached to عجلت; رب is a vocative (munādā) annexed to the omitted yāʾ of the first person, with the vocative particle omitted. لترضى: the lām is for giving the reason and ترضى is an imperfect verb in the accusative (manṣūb) by an implied أن after the lām of reason; the preposition and its genitive noun are also attached to عجلت, as if it were the reason for his haste.
(قالَ فَإِنَّا قَدْ فَتَنَّا قَوْمَكَ مِنْ بَعْدِكَ وَأَضَلَّهُمُ السَّامِرِيُّ): قال is a past verb whose fāʿil is latent, referring to Allah; the fāʾ is the fāʾ al-faṣīḥa, i.e. "if you wish to know the fate of your people"; إنّ and its ism, and the clause قد فتنا is its khabar, being a verb and its fāʿil; قومك is the mafʿūl bihi; أضلهم السامري is a verb, a fronted mafʿūl bihi and a postponed fāʿil.
(فَرَجَعَ مُوسى إِلى قَوْمِهِ غَضْبانَ أَسِفاً): It has already been said about the fāʾ of immediate sequence that it may lag in its timing without an interval occurring; for Moses did not return until after he had completed the forty days and received the Torah. رجع is a past verb and موسى is the fāʿil; إلى قومه is attached to رجع; غضبان and أسفا are two ḥāls.
(قالَ يا قَوْمِ أَلَمْ يَعِدْكُمْ رَبُّكُمْ وَعْداً حَسَناً): يا is a vocative particle and قوم is a vocative annexed to the omitted yāʾ of the first person. ألم: the hamza is for the interrogative of disapproval; يعدكم is an imperfect verb in the jussive (majzūm) by لم; the kāf is the mafʿūl bihi and ربكم is the fāʿil; وعدا is a mafʿūl muṭlaq (absolute object) and حسنا is a naʿt (adjective).
(أَفَطالَ عَلَيْكُمُ الْعَهْدُ أَمْ أَرَدْتُمْ أَنْ يَحِلَّ عَلَيْكُمْ غَضَبٌ مِنْ رَبِّكُمْ فَأَخْلَفْتُمْ مَوْعِدِي): The hamza is for interrogation and the fāʾ is a conjunction conjoining to something omitted; طال is a past verb, عليكم is attached to طال, and العهد is the fāʿil; أم is a conjunction counterbalancing the hamza; أردتم is a verb and its fāʿil; أن and what is within its scope are the object of أردتم; عليكم is attached to يحل; غضب is the fāʿil of يحل, and من ربكم is a naʿt of غضب. فأخلفتم: the fāʾ is a conjunction and أخلفتم is conjoined to أردتم; موعدي is the object of أخلفتم.

* Rhetoric:
Interrogation from Allah the Exalted does not occur to seek knowledge; rather it departs from its original meaning for other purposes which are grasped from the context of the speech. The question here has conveyed purposes which we summarise below:
a- To inform the one asked of matters of which he is ignorant: He, Glorified is He, wished to inform him of the trial of his people. It is said that they numbered about six hundred thousand souls, and none of them escaped the worship of the calf except twelve thousand.
b- To rebuke the one asked, make him understand, and alert him to the error of what he did in leaving the people and giving room to al-Sāmirī to lead them astray, since he was steeped in misguidance and skilled in misleading.
c- To teach the one asked the etiquette of travel, which is that the leader of a people ought to stay behind them on the march, so that his gaze encompasses them, penetrates them and watches over them, and so that he cuts off the path to every trial that might slip into their ranks.
However, Moses, upon him be peace, neglected these matters — and perhaps he was acquainted with them and aware of them — but longing for the meeting with Allah and hastening to His appointment set his heart aflame, so that he could not hold the reins of his unruly patience. Such is the state of one promised something he has long yearned for: he wishes he could ride on the wings of birds and outrun the hours. And is there anything that inflames longing like an appointment with Allah?

dervis-irab:17-23.t:
* Vocabulary:
(أَهُشُّ): in al-Miṣbāḥ: هشّ الرجل هشّا, of the ردّ pattern: he made a sweeping motion with his stick; in the Revelation: «وَأَهُشُّ بِها عَلى غَنَمِي». هش الشجرة هشا: he beat the tree so that its leaves would fall. هش الشيء يهش, of the تعب pattern, هشاشة: it became soft and slack, so it is هش; هش العود يهشّ also, هشوشا: the stick became brittle, quick to break; and هش الرجل هشاشة, when he smiled, of the تعب and ضرب patterns.
(جَناحِكَ): its explanation will come in the section on Rhetoric.

* I'rab:
(وَما تِلْكَ بِيَمِينِكَ يا مُوسى): the wāw is a conjunction; ما is an interrogative noun for affirmation (taqrīr), the mubtadaʾ (subject); تلك is its khabar (predicate); بيمينك is attached to (mutaʿalliq) an omitted ḥāl (circumstantial). It resembles the saying of the Exalted «وَهذا بَعْلِي شَيْخاً»; what governs the implied ḥāl is the demonstrative. يا موسى is a vocative. So ما is an indefinite noun in the position of the nominative as mubtadaʾ, the implied form being "what thing is that in your right hand?"; it is indeclinable (mabnī) because it contains the meaning of the interrogative hamza. It was brought for a kind of brevity: when you say "What is in your hand?", it is as though you said "Is it a stick in your hand, or a sword, or a dagger?" and the like of what might be in his hand, and he would not be obliged to answer you about what is in his hand if you did not hit upon what was intended. So they brought ما, a noun that applies to everything non-rational, vague in it, and made it contain the interrogative hamza; so it required an answer from the very first, and so it contains the conciseness you see.
(قالَ: هِيَ عَصايَ أَتَوَكَّؤُا عَلَيْها وَأَهُشُّ بِها عَلى غَنَمِي): هي is a mubtadaʾ and عصاي its khabar; the clause أتوكأ عليها is a ḥāl, and it was also said to be resumptive; أهش بها على غنمي is conjoined to أتوكأ عليها; بها is attached to أهش, and likewise على غنمي. Making أهش transitive with على conveys the sense of alarming and frightening the sheep.
(وَلِيَ فِيها مَآرِبُ أُخْرى): this is the fourth answer with which Moses answered a single question; the secret of that will come in the section on Rhetoric. لي is a fronted khabar; فيها is a ḥāl; مآرب, the plural of مأربة (with any of the three vowels on the rāʾ), is a postponed mubtadaʾ; and أخرى is an adjective of مآرب. A large part of these "other uses" will come in the section on Rhetoric, together with a useful summary of al-Jāḥiẓ's Book of the Staff (Kitāb al-ʿAṣā).
(قالَ: أَلْقِها يا مُوسى): the clause ألقها is the object of the saying (maqūl al-qawl), and يا موسى is a vocative.
(فَأَلْقاها فَإِذا هِيَ حَيَّةٌ تَسْعى): ألقاها is a verb, its agent and its object; the fāʾ is a conjunction; إذا is for surprise (mufājaʾa) — whether it is an adverb or a particle has been discussed earlier in detail. هي is a mubtadaʾ and حية the khabar; the clause تسعى is a ḥāl or a second khabar. The mention of the "hornet question" (al-masʾala al-zunbūriyya) between Sībawayh and al-Kisāʾī has preceded.
(قالَ خُذْها وَلا تَخَفْ سَنُعِيدُها سِيرَتَهَا الْأُولى): the clause خذها is the object of the saying; the wāw is a conjunction; لا is prohibitive; تخف is an imperfect verb in the jussive (majzūm) by prohibitive لا. The sīn is a particle of the future; نعيدها is an imperfect verb whose agent is latent (mustatir), its implied form being "We"; سيرتها is accusative by removal of the preposition (manṣūb bi-nazʿ al-khāfiḍ), i.e. "to its state" — this is the simplest of the parsings. It was also said that it is an adverb; they said: "السيرة is from السير (going), like الركبة from الركوب; one says 'so-and-so went a good way (سيرة)'; then it was extended and transferred to the sense of way and manner; and it was said 'the way of the ancients'. So it was made accusative as an adverb, i.e. We will restore it in its first manner." Others, such as Abū al-Baqāʾ — and he began with it — allowed it to be a badal ishtimāl (substitute of inclusion) of the object pronoun, because the meaning of سيرتها is its description and manner. al-Zamakhsharī brought another parsing, which he prepared for and commended; he said: "A third, fine aspect is that سنعيدها stands on its own, not connected with سيرتها, in the sense that it was originally created as a staff, then departed and was nullified by being turned into a snake; so We will restore it after its departure as We created it at first; and سيرتها is accusative by an implied verb, i.e. it will go its first way (تسير سيرتها الأولى)." In any case الأولى is an adjective of سيرتها.
(وَاضْمُمْ يَدَكَ إِلى جَناحِكَ تَخْرُجْ بَيْضاءَ مِنْ غَيْرِ سُوءٍ آيَةً أُخْرى): اضمم is conjoined to ألقها; يدك is the mafʿūl bihi (direct object), and the agent is latent, its implied form being "you"; إلى جناحك, a preposition and its genitive noun, is attached to اضمم. تخرج is jussive because it is the answer to the command (jawāb al-ṭalab); بيضاء is a ḥāl; من غير سوء is attached to بيضاء because of the verbal sense in it, as in "it became white without harm", and so that the iḥtirās (precaution) may be complete, as will come in the section on Rhetoric; or it is attached to تخرج. آية is likewise a second ḥāl of the agent of تخرج, and أخرى is an adjective of آية. al-Zamakhsharī chose another aspect for the accusative of آية, namely "by implying something like خذ ['take'] [Translator's note: the source has خذأ], دونك ['here, take'] and the like" — and we see no need for that.
(لِنُرِيَكَ مِنْ آياتِنَا الْكُبْرى): the lām is for cause (taʿlīl); نريك is an imperfect verb in the accusative (manṣūb) by an implied أن after the lām; it gives the reason for something omitted to which it is attached, i.e. "We commanded you what We mentioned so that We might show you by it", i.e. by your hand. من آياتنا is attached to an omitted element as a ḥāl of الكبرى; on this view الكبرى is the second object of نريك, or, more correctly, an adjective of the second object, the implied form being "so that We may show you the greatest sign from among Our signs", i.e. being one of Our signs. Other things were said, but what we have mentioned is preferable, so there is no need to mention them.

* Rhetoric:
This verse could fill enormous volumes because of the kinds of eloquence it contains — and that is what our book aims at; but we shall be as brief as possible, and so we say:
1- The device of al-talfīf (wrapping):
In the saying of the Exalted «وَما تِلْكَ بِيَمِينِكَ يا مُوسى», up to the end of the four answers with which Moses, the blessings of Allah be upon him, answered, there is an elegant device not mentioned until now: the device of talfīf. Its definition is presenting words in the form of instruction in a ruling or a point of conduct which the speaker did not [explicitly] intend to mention, but rather intended to mention a particular ruling falling within the generality of the stated ruling whose teaching he made explicit. We believe this lengthy definition needs clarification, namely: the questioner asks about a ruling that is one species of a genus, all or most of whose species need to be explained; so the one asked turns away from the specific answer explaining that species he was asked about, and answers with a general answer which includes clarification of the ruling asked about and of others, because of the need to explain it. Moses's saying, in answer to Allah the Exalted's question to him, «هِيَ عَصايَ»,
is the actual answer to the question. Then he said «أتوكأ عليها وأهش بها على غنمي ولي فيها مآرب أخرى», thereby answering an implied question, as though he imagined being asked: "And what do you do with it?" So he spoke, enumerating its uses. This came from Moses, peace be upon him, only for three reasons:
a- Seeking to give thanks to Allah the Exalted, who had provided him with that staff, in which he found uses not found in its like.
b- The setting is one of speaking with the Beloved, which calls for expansiveness and elaboration.
c- [He regarded as] momentous his Lord's asking him about its uses, so he began by answering the implied question before it occurred, out of courtesy towards his Lord.
In fact, when a question is put about something evident, that question is directed only at some matter connected with it, according to what the situation requires; otherwise it would be pointless, since the thing is evident. For example, if you ask someone wearing travelling clothes, "What is this garment?", you are not asking about the garment itself and its nature, but only about the reason for wearing it; so it is as though you said, "What is the reason for your resolve?" The wearer's answer then is to say:
"I intend such-and-such a journey." If he answered that it is linen, for example, he would be considered to be talking nonsense. So likewise here: since the question was about an evident matter, it is directed at what is connected with the staff, namely its uses; so it is as if He said, "What do you do with what is in your right hand, O Moses?" For that reason he said «هي عصاي أتوكأ عليها» … to the end of the verse. If you say: if the saying of the Exalted «وما تلك بيمينك» were a question about something connected with the staff [Translator's note: the source has عما لا يتعلق, "about what is not connected", which seems inconsistent with the argument], then the proper answer would be to say "I intend to lean on it and beat down leaves with it for my sheep", and his saying «هي عصاي» would be wasted and not match the question — as in the question about travelling dress [Translator's note: the source has نبس, a misprint for لبس].
I say: although this question is about what is connected with the staff, since He, Exalted, knew that the form of a serpent would come upon it at the time of the sorcerers' magic, and that would be an occasion for Moses to fear on seeing an abhorrent form he was unfamiliar with, He wished to fix its nature and its attributes in his mind so that he would not be bewildered when it came upon him. For that reason He said «ما تلك», so that he would answer about its nature as well as about its uses, for greater firmness. The gist of the answer's meaning is then: "It is my staff; I know it in its essence and its attributes; its form is established in my mind; it serves only the uses of its like, for I have long leaned on it, beaten down leaves with it for my sheep [Translator's note: the source has عنمي, a misprint for غنمي], and I have other uses for it."
He chose تلك (the distal demonstrative) although what is pointed to is near, either to belittle it in relation to the majesty of His grandeur, or to magnify it, since it contained wondrous matters and many uses.

2- al-Taqrīr (eliciting affirmation):
It also contains taqrīr, which is by means of the interrogative; for He, Glorified, knows what is in his right hand, but He wished Moses to affirm and acknowledge its being a staff, and his knowledge of what Allah would grant him in his staff to increase, so that no doubt would come upon him when Allah turned it into a serpent; rather he would know that this happens by the power of Allah and that it is light and easy for Him.

The staff of Moses and the sayings about it:
al-Jāḥiẓ composed a book which he called The Book of the Staff, and it is of great benefit; we cite below some collected portions of it. Allah gathered for Moses son of ʿImrān in his staff great proofs and mighty signs such as might suffice for the signs of a number of messengers. Allah, Blessed and Exalted, said in what He mentions about his staff:
«إِنْ هذانِ لَساحِرانِ يُرِيدانِ أَنْ يُخْرِجاكُمْ مِنْ أَرْضِكُمْ بِسِحْرِهِما» up to His saying «ولا يفلح الساحر حيث أتى». For this reason al-Ḥasan ibn Hāniʾ — Abū Nuwās — said concerning Khaṣīb and the people of Egypt when they rose in turmoil against him:
منحتكم يا أهل مصر نصيحتي ... ألا فخذوا من ناصح بنصيب
ولا تثبوا وثب السفاه فتركبوا ... على حد حامي الظهر غير ركوب
فإن يك باق إفك فرعون فيكم ... فإن عصا موسى بكف خصيب
رماكم أمير المؤمنين بحية ... أكول لحيات البلاد شروب
(I have given you my advice, O people of Egypt — so take a share from an adviser; do not leap the leap of folly and so mount the edge of a [beast] with a guarded back, unfit for riding. If the lie of Pharaoh still remains among you, then the staff of Moses is in the hand of Khaṣīb. The Commander of the Faithful has hurled at you a serpent that devours and swallows the serpents of the land.)
Do you not see that the sorcerers did not undertake to mislead people and deceive them except with staffs, and that Moses did not oppose them except with his staff? Do you not see that when they bewitched people's eyes and terrified them with staffs and ropes, Allah did not give the ropes the merit in bringing a proof that He gave the staff? Yet Allah's power to turn ropes in various ways is like His power to turn the staff.
Then al-Jāḥiẓ, in his sweet and generous style, spoke about trees and their uses, which will be referred to in due course, and cited transmitted stories about the use of the staff and the importance it had among the Arabs. He cited the story of ʿĀmir ibn al-Ẓarib al-ʿAdwānī — the arbiter of the Arabs in the Jāhiliyya: when he grew old and forgetfulness came over him, he ordered his daughter ʿAmra to knock with the staff whenever he faltered in judgement and deviated from the right course. She was one of the wise daughters of the Arabs, surpassing in that the standing of Ṣuḥr bint Luqmān, Hind bint al-Khuss and Jumʿa bint Ḥābis. ʿĀmir was called "the man of forbearance" (dhū al-ḥilm). For this reason al-Ḥārith ibn Waʿla said:
وزعمتم أن لا حلوم لنا ... إن العصا قرعت لذي الحلم
(You claimed that we have no forbearance — the staff was knocked for the man of forbearance.)
And al-Farazdaq said:
فإن كنت أنساني حلوم مجاشع ... فإن العصا كانت لذي الحلم تقرع
(If the forbearance of Mujāshiʿ has made me forget, the staff used to be knocked for the man of forbearance.)

I say:
I say: this is what al-Jāḥiẓ related concerning knocking with the staff, but this account is not decisive; there is lengthy disagreement about the first person for whom the staff was knocked. It was said to be ʿĀmir ibn al-Ẓarib, as al-Jāḥiẓ mentioned; it was said to be Qays ibn Khālid Dhū al-Jaddayn; and it was said to be ʿAmr ibn Ḥumama al-Dawsī. But the best known is what al-Jāḥiẓ related.
The mention of the staff among them runs in many senses. The Arabs say: "The staff is from the little stick (العصيّة), and the viper is the daughter of a snake", meaning that a great matter arises from a small one. One says: "So-and-so's staff flew into splinters"; and one says: "So-and-so split the staff of the Muslims", and one does not say "split a garment" or anything else to which the word "splitting" applies. al-Muḍarris al-Asadī said:
وألقت عصاها واستقر بها النوى ... كما قر عينا بالإياب المسافر
(She threw down her staff and her destination settled her, as the traveller is gladdened by his return.)
The Banū Asad are called "slaves of the staff", meaning that they submit to every chief with whom they make an alliance. The Arabs call everyone with a small head "the staff"; ʿAmr ibn Hubayra had a small head, and Suwayd ibn Kurāʿ al-ʿUklī said:
فمن مبلغ رأس العصا أن بيننا ... ضغائن لا تنسى وإن قدم الدهر
(Who will tell Staff-head that between us are grudges not forgotten, however old time grows?)
Wāliba ibn al-Ḥubāb al-Asadī was one of those from whom Abū Nuwās learned; he was a ribald poet with a small head. Abū al-ʿAtāhiya said about the head of Wāliba and the heads of his people:
رؤوس عصي كنّ من عود أثلة ... لها قادح يفري وآخر مخرب
(Heads of staffs made from tamarisk wood, with a worm boring into them and another hollowing them out.)
I say:
I say: Wāliba had exchanged satires with Bashshār and Abū al-ʿAtāhiya, and they defeated him, and he fled from them to Kufa. Among what he said about Abū al-ʿAtāhiya:
كان فينا يكنى أبا اسحق ... وبها الركب سار في الآفاق
فتكنى معتها بعتاه ... يا لها كنية أتت باتفاق
حلق الله لحية لك لا تنفك معقودة بداء الحلاق
(Among us he used to be called Abū Isḥāq, and with that name caravans travelled through the horizons; then, being an idiot, he took the kunya of ʿAtāh (madness) — what a kunya, come by chance! May Allah shave a beard of yours that is ever knotted with the disease of shaving.)
ʿAmr ibn Saʿd ibn Abī Waqqāṣ [Translator's note: so in the source; the well-known version of this story concerns ʿUmayr ibn Saʿd] came in to ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb when he returned to him from the governorship of Ḥimṣ, having with him nothing but a bag, a water-skin, a bowl and a staff. ʿUmar said to him: "What is this bad state I see you in — or what are you doing?" He said:
"And what is it that you see of me? Do you not see me sound of body, having the world with all it contains?"
He said: "And what do you have of the world?" He said: "I have my bag in which I carry my provisions; I have my bowl in which I wash my clothes; I have my water-skin in which I carry my water for drinking; and I have my staff: if I meet an enemy I fight him, and if I meet a snake I kill it. What remains of the world is subordinate to what I have."
Among the fine sayings about the staff and the uses and benefits it may serve is the explanation of the poetry of Ghunya the Bedouin woman about her son. She had a son of great ferocity who was always provoking people, despite a weak frame and thin bones. Once he leapt upon a young Bedouin, and the young man cut off his nose; Ghunya took the blood-money for his nose, and her situation improved after grinding poverty. Then he leapt upon another, who cut off his ear; she took the blood-money, and the blood-money for his ear increased her wealth and improved her situation. Then after that he leapt upon another, who cut off his lip. When she saw the camels, sheep, goods and earnings she had acquired through her son's limbs, her opinion of him improved, and she mentioned him in a rajaz poem of hers, saying in it:
أحلف بالمروة حقا والصفا ... أنك خير من تفاريق العصا
(I swear truly by al-Marwa and al-Ṣafā that you are better than the pieces of a staff.)
Ibn al-Aʿrābī was asked: "What are the pieces of a staff?" He said: "The staff is cut into a dog-collar stick (ساجور); the stick of the collar is cut and becomes tent-pegs; the peg is split and each piece becomes a sack-pin (شظاظ); if the head of the pin is like a lump, it becomes a nose-peg (مهار) for a Bactrian camel — the piece of wood inserted into the nose of the Bactrian camel (the Bactrian being the Khurāsānī camel); and when the nose-peg is split, small pegs [Translator's note: the source has تواد] come from it. The collar-sticks are for dogs and for human captives."
And he was asked about His saying «ولي فيها مآرب أخرى». He said: "I cannot encompass all the uses of Moses, peace be upon him, but I will tell you some general things that fall under the need for a staff. Among them: it is carried against the snake, the scorpion, the wolf, the stallion in rut, and the wild ass of the herd in the season when the stallions are excited, and likewise the stallions of burrows [Translator's note: so in the source, الجحور] in the meadows. The very old man, the persistently ill one, the one whose leg is cut off and the lame lean on it, for it takes the place of another leg." A Bedouin whose leg had been cut off said:
الله يعلم أني من رجالهم ... وإن تخدّد عن متنيّ أطماري
وإن رزئت يدا كانت تجمّلني ... وإن مشيت على زج ومسمار
(Allah knows that I am one of their men, even if my rags are torn from my back, even if I have lost a hand that used to adorn me, and even if I walk on a spike and a nail.)
"The staff stands in for the blind man's guide. It is for the fuller, the fāshkār [Translator's note: so in the source] and the tanner; from it is made the poker for the hot ashes (i.e. the piece of wood with which hot ashes are stirred) and the stirrer for the oven. It is for pounding plaster, gypsum and sesame, and for beating down leaves from trees; and for the runner (the courier of the post and of the state) and for the hirer of animals, for both take walking sticks, and when the stretch is long and the goal distant, they help themselves in their running and trotting many times over by leaning on the face of the ground. It straightens the lean of the paralysed and steadies the trembling of one with birsām (one afflicted with the disease of pleurisy). The shepherd takes it for his sheep, and every rider for his mount. A man puts his staff through the loop of his provision bag and holds the other end with his hand; sometimes one end is in the hand of one man and the other end in the hand of his companion, with a heavy load on it. It may be — if you wish — a peg in a wall; if you wish you plant it in open ground and make it a qibla [marker]; if you wish you make it a shade; if you put a spike on it, it becomes a short spear (ʿanaza); if you add something to it, it becomes a crutch; if you add something to it, it becomes a javelin; and if you add something to it, it becomes a lance. And the staff serves as a whip and a weapon."
We content ourselves with what has preceded from al-Jāḥiẓ's book and return to the uses of Moses. It is mentioned in al-Kashshāf: "It was said about the uses: it had two prongs and a crook; when a branch was high he bent it down with the crook, and when he wanted to break it he twisted it with the two prongs; when he travelled he put it on his shoulder and hung his gear on it — the bow, the quiver, the milking pail and others; when he was in the open country he planted it, laid the two fire-sticks across its two prongs, threw his cloak over it and sat in its shade; when his rope was too short he lengthened it with it; and he used to fight off wild beasts from his sheep with it [Translator's note: the source has غمه, a misprint for غنمه]."

3- The implied metaphor (al-istiʿāra al-makniyya):
In His saying «وَاضْمُمْ يَدَكَ إِلى جَناحِكَ»: الجناح (wing) is well known; any two sides are called two wings, like the two wings of an army; a person's two wings are his two sides; and the original from which the metaphor is borrowed is a bird's two wings, called جناحان because it inclines them (يجنحهما) when flying, i.e. tilts them. What is meant is "to your side, under the upper arm"; His saying تخرج indicates that.
4- Precaution (al-iḥtirās) and metonymy (al-kināya):
In His saying «تَخْرُجْ بَيْضاءَ مِنْ غَيْرِ سُوءٍ» there is the device of iḥtirās, which has been mentioned before. السوء is badness and ugliness in anything; it is used here as a metonymy for leprosy (البرص), just as العورة (the private parts) is referred to by metonymy as السوءة. Jadhīma ibn al-Waḍḍāḥ was leprous, so they referred to him by metonymy as al-Abrash (the speckled), because leprosy was the most hateful thing to the Arabs and they had a frowning aversion to it, so it deserved to be referred to by metonymy. And nothing is finer or more delicate than the metonymies of the Quran, as will come. Had He not mentioned «من غير سوء», it might have been imagined that the whiteness had increased until it became leprosy, so He brought His saying «من غير سوء» to ward off that misconception.

dervis-irab:24-35.t:
* Vocabulary:
(وَزِيراً): derived from الوزر (burden), because he bears the king's burdens (أوزاره), i.e. his loads, so he is a helper in the king's affairs and one who undertakes his business. It was also said rather that it is derived from الوَزَر, with two fatḥas, which is a refuge; from it is the saying of the Exalted «كَلَّا لا وَزَرَ». It was also said rather that it is derived from المؤازرة, which is mutual help. In al-Qāmūs: الأزر is encompassing, strength and weakness — so it is one of the aḍdād (words with opposite meanings) — and strengthening, and the back.

* I'rab:
(اذْهَبْ إِلى فِرْعَوْنَ إِنَّهُ طَغى): اذهب is an imperative verb whose fāʿil (agent) is latent (mustatir), its implied form being "you"; إلى فرعون is attached to (mutaʿalliq) اذهب; إن and its noun, and the clause طغى is its khabar (predicate); the clause إنه طغى gives the reason and has no grammatical position.
(قالَ رَبِّ اشْرَحْ لِي صَدْرِي): قال is a past verb whose agent is latent, its implied form being "he"; رب is a vocative annexed to the omitted first-person yāʾ; اشرح is a verb of supplication; لي is attached to اشرح; and صدري is the mafʿūl bihi (direct object). The word لي is mentioned for a benefit that will come in the section on Rhetoric.
(وَيَسِّرْ لِي أَمْرِي): conjoined to اشرح لي صدري.
(وَاحْلُلْ عُقْدَةً مِنْ لِسانِي): conjoined to اشرح; عقدة is a direct object; من لساني is attached to an omitted adjective of عقدة, as if it were said "a knot from among the knots of my tongue". What has been said about the knot will come in the section on Rhetoric.
(يَفْقَهُوا قَوْلِي): يفقهوا is an imperfect verb in the jussive (majzūm) because it is the answer to the request (jawāb al-ṭalab); the wāw is the agent; and قولي is a direct object.
(وَاجْعَلْ لِي وَزِيراً مِنْ أَهْلِي) (هارُونَ أَخِي): the wāw is a conjunction; اجعل is an imperative verb whose agent is latent, its implied form being "you"; لي is in the position of the accusative as the second object; وزيرا is the first object; من أهلي is an adjective of وزيرا; هارون is a badal (substitute) of وزيرا; and أخي is a badal of هارون. It is also possible that وزيرا is the second object and هارون the first object, the second being placed before it out of concern for the matter of the vizierate; لي is then attached to an omitted ḥāl (circumstantial), or to the "making" itself, and من أهلي is an adjective. It is also possible that وزيرا is the first object and من أهلي the second. All these aspects are equally weighty.
(اشْدُدْ بِهِ أَزْرِي) (وَأَشْرِكْهُ فِي أَمْرِي): اشدد is a verb of supplication whose agent is a latent pronoun, its implied form being "you"; به is attached to اشدد; أزري is a direct object; أشركه is conjoined to اشدد, the hāʾ being the direct object; and في أمري is attached to أشركه. It was also read أَشدد and أُشركه, as imperfect verbs in the jussive by the request.
(كَيْ نُسَبِّحَكَ كَثِيراً) (وَنَذْكُرَكَ كَثِيراً): كي is a particle of maṣdar, of the accusative and of the future; its discussion will come in the section on Benefits. نسبحك is an imperfect verb in the accusative (manṣūb) by كي, and the agent of نسبحك is a latent pronoun, its implied form being "we". كثيرا is an adjective of an omitted maṣdar (verbal noun) or an adjective of an omitted adverb, so it is a mafʿūl muṭlaq (absolute object) or a mafʿūl fīhi (adverbial). نذكرك كثيرا is conjoined to نسبحك كثيرا.
(إِنَّكَ كُنْتَ بِنا بَصِيراً): إن and its noun, and the clause كنت is the khabar; the tāʾ is the noun of كنت; بنا is attached to بصيرا; and بصيرا is the khabar of كنت.

* Rhetoric:
1- Addition (al-ziyāda):
The addition of لي in the saying of the Exalted «رَبِّ اشْرَحْ لِي صَدْرِي وَيَسِّرْ لِي أَمْرِي», although the sentence is complete without it. al-Zamakhsharī mentioned one secret [of it], and we will mention the second afterwards. He said: "If you ask: what is the use of لي in His saying اشرح لي صدري ويسر لي أمري, when the sentence is in good order without it? I say: the sentence was first made vague, so it was said 'expand for me' and 'ease for me', and it became known that there was something to be expanded and something to be eased; then it was made clear and the vagueness removed by mentioning them, so it was more emphatic in requesting the expansion and easing for his breast and his affair." As for the second secret, it is that its benefit is the acknowledgement that the benefit of the expansion of the breast and the easing of the affair returns to him and redounds upon him; for Allah, Mighty and Majestic, does not benefit from sending him, nor does He seek help through the expansion of his breast — Exalted and Holy is He.

2- Indefiniteness (al-tankīr):
The indefiniteness of العقدة in the saying of the Exalted «وَاحْلُلْ عُقْدَةً مِنْ لِسانِي» indicates that he did not ask Him to undo all the knots of his tongue, but rather to undo some of them — the one that prevented making himself understood — as shown by his saying «يفقهوا قولي»; as though he said "and undo a knot from among the knots of my tongue". This knot arose, as is narrated, from a live coal that he put in his mouth when he was small; its story is in the lengthy works.

* Benefits:
A discussion of كي:
(كَيْ) is one of the particles of the accusative, and it is of two kinds:
1- The maṣdariyya (infinitival) kay, which is the one preceded by the lām, either in wording, as in لكي لا تأسوا, or by implication, as in جئتك كي تكرمني, if you estimate the original as لكي and that you have dropped the lām, dispensing with it by intending it. If you do not estimate the lām, then it is:
2- The kay of cause (al-taʿlīliyya). The maṣdariyya puts [the verb] in the accusative by itself; the taʿlīliyya is genitive-governing, and what puts [the verb] in the accusative after it is an implied أن, necessarily implied in prose, though it may appear in poetry:
فقالت أكل الناس أصبحت مانحا ... لسانك كيما ان تغرّ وتخدعا
(She said: "Have you come to give your tongue to all people, in order to deceive and beguile?")
This is the doctrine of Sībawayh, al-Khalīl and the majority of the Basrans. As for the Kufans, they hold that كي always puts [the verb] in the accusative, whether or not the lām precedes it.
Abū Ḥayyān said: they agreed that it is permissible to separate it from what it governs by negating لا and redundant (zāʾida) ما; as for separation by anything other than what was mentioned, it is not permissible according to the Basrans.

dervis-irab:87-98.t:
* Vocabulary:
(بِمَلْكِنا): by our power; the maṣdar (verbal noun) of ملك, whose mīm may take any of the three vowels. In al-Qāmūs and its commentary al-Tāj: «ملك يملك, of the pattern taʿiba, malkan, mulkan and milkan, with fatḥa, ḍamma and kasra on the mīm, and malaka and mamlaka with fatḥa on the lām, and mamlika with kasra on it, and mamluka with ḍamma on it: he took possession of the thing, being able to dispose of it and to have it exclusively. ملك على القوم: he gained mastery over the people. ملك على فلان أمره: it took hold of him. ملك نفسه: he was able to restrain himself. ملك المرأة: he married the woman».
(أَوْزاراً): burdens. By it they meant the jewellery of the Copts which they had borrowed from them; and by awzār they meant that it was sins and liabilities, because they had borrowed it from them and had no right to it.
(خُوارٌ): with ḍamma on the khāʾ, the sound of cattle and calves. He expressed it with جسد (body) even though it is not said of a rational being [Translator's note: the sentence is garbled in the source, which reads «مع أنه لا يقال للعاقل: ولأن الجسد لا يقال إلا للانسان»; the intended sense seems to be that jasad is said only of humans]; and because jasad is only said of a human, it is by way of predominance (taghlīb) and likening it to a rational being, as if it were different from cattle. Jasad is not said of anything other than a human except of saffron — it is also called jasād, with fatḥa on the jīm — and of blood when it has dried, which is also called jāsid.
(يَا بْنَ أُمَّ): this will come in the section on Benefits [Translator's note: it is in fact treated in the I'rab section below].
(فَقَبَضْتُ): قبض يقبض, of the pattern jalasa, the thing with his hand, and on the thing: he held it in his hand and closed his fingers on it. قبض يده عن الشيء: he refrained from holding it. قبضه عن الأمر: he turned him away from it. قبضه الله: Allah caused him to die. قبض الشيء: the opposite of spreading it out and widening it. قبض الطائر جناحه: the bird drew its wing together. قبض الدار ونحوها: he took delivery of the house and the like. قبض منه المال: he took the money from him for himself. قبض قبضة: he took a handful. One also says قبص, with the unpointed ṣād, because the two alternate in many words, the most important of which we cite below:
Yaʿqūb ibn al-Sikkīt said: «قبضت قبضة [Translator's note: printed «وقضت قبضة»] and قبصت قبصة», and it is said that al-qabṣa is less than al-qabḍa. Another said: al-qabṣ is with the fingertips and al-qabḍ is with the whole palm. One says «عاد إلى ضئضئه وصئصئه», i.e. he returned to his origin, and the hamza is original. He recited:
أنا من ضئضىء صدق ... بخ ومن أكرم حذل
(I am from a true stock — bravo! — and from the noblest root.)
من عزاني قال به به ... سنخ ذا أكرم أصل
(Whoever traces my descent says: "Bravo, bravo! The origin of this one is the noblest of roots.")
Al-ḥidhl is the stone [Translator's note: as printed; al-ḥidhl is usually glossed as "origin, root"]. Al-Liḥyānī said: «بخ بخ» and «به به» are said to a person when he is extolled. Abū ʿAmr said: «ما ينوض بحاجة» and «ما يقدر على أن ينوص», i.e. to move; from it is the saying of the Mighty and Majestic: «وَلاتَ حِينَ مَناصٍ»; manāṣ and manāḍ are one. One says أنقاص and أنقاض with one meaning. Al-Aṣmaʿī said: al-munqāḍ is what is uprooted from its root, and al-munqāṣ is what is split lengthwise. He also said: «مضمض لسانه» and «مصمص لسانه» when he moved it. Al-Liḥyānī said: one says «إنه لصلّ أصلال» and «ضلّ أضلال»; al-ṣill is the snake which kills instantly when it bites. One says «مصمص إناءه» and «مضمضه» when he washed it; so the common people's saying «مصمص العظم» (he sucked the bone) is correct and beyond reproach.
(بَصُرْتُ): بصر بالشيء, with ḍamma on the ṣād, and أبصره, meaning he knew it; it is of the pattern ẓarufa. One also says بصر, with kasra, of the pattern ʿalima.
(مِساسَ): with kasra on the mīm, the maṣdar of ماسّ. The reality of this construction will come in the I'rab section.

* I'rab:
(قالُوا ما أَخْلَفْنا مَوْعِدَكَ بِمَلْكِنا): قالوا is a verb and its fāʿil (agent); ما is negative; أخلفنا is a verb and its fāʿil; موعدك is the mafʿūl bihi (direct object); بملكنا is a preposition and its genitive noun attached to (mutaʿalliq) an omitted ḥāl (circumstantial), i.e. "while we were masters of our affair", but we were overcome in our affair on the part of al-Sāmirī and his scheme.
(وَلكِنَّا حُمِّلْنا أَوْزاراً مِنْ زِينَةِ الْقَوْمِ): The wāw is a conjunction; لكنّ and its ism; حملنا is a past verb in the passive, and نا is the nāʾib fāʿil (deputy agent); أوزارا is the second mafʿūl bihi, and من زينة القوم is a naʿt (adjective).
(فَقَذَفْناها فَكَذلِكَ أَلْقَى السَّامِرِيُّ): The fāʾ is a conjunction; قذفناها is a verb, its fāʿil and its object; it is conjoined to something omitted, i.e. "so al-Sāmirī said to us: throw it into the fire, because Moses has delayed coming to you on account of it; so we threw it". The fāʾ is a conjunction; كذلك is a naʿt of an omitted maṣdar, as has often been given; ألقى السامري is a verb and its fāʿil.
(فَأَخْرَجَ لَهُمْ عِجْلًا جَسَداً لَهُ خُوارٌ): The fāʾ is a conjunction; أخرج is a past verb whose fāʿil is latent (mustatir), its implied form being "he", referring to al-Sāmirī; the conjunction is to «فأضلهم السامري», so that it should not be imagined that it is part of their speech. لهم is attached to أخرج; عجلا is the mafʿūl bihi, and جسدا is a ḥāl of عجلا. But a difficulty with this parsing, which a number of the commentators chose, is that the one to whom the ḥāl refers (ṣāḥib al-ḥāl) can only be definite. Perhaps this calf, which al-Sāmirī brought out of the pit in which was the earth from the track of the hoof of the messenger to Moses, as will come, came to have the status of a definite noun. We say: there is nothing to prevent parsing it as a badal (substitute) from عجلا. The clause له خوار, consisting of a fronted khabar (predicate) and a postponed mubtadaʾ (subject), is a naʿt.
(فَقالُوا هذا إِلهُكُمْ وَإِلهُ مُوسى فَنَسِيَ): The fāʾ is a conjunction; قالوا is a verb and its fāʿil; هذا is a mubtadaʾ and إلهكم is the khabar; إله موسى is conjoined to إلهكم. فنسي: the fāʾ is a conjunction and نسي is a past verb whose fāʿil is latent, its implied form being "he", referring to Moses, i.e. he forgot his Lord and went to seek Him. It is also said that the pronoun refers to al-Sāmirī, i.e. he abandoned the outward faith he had been upon.
(أَفَلا يَرَوْنَ أَلَّا يَرْجِعُ إِلَيْهِمْ قَوْلًا وَلا يَمْلِكُ لَهُمْ ضَرًّا وَلا نَفْعاً): The hamza is for interrogation and the fāʾ is a conjunction; لا is negative; يرون is an imperfect verb in the nominative (marfūʿ) by the retention of the nūn, and the wāw is the fāʿil; أن is lightened from the heavy (anna), لا is negative and يرجع is an imperfect verb; the ism of the lightened أن is the pronoun of the matter (ḍamīr al-shaʾn), i.e. «أنه»; the fāʿil of يرجع is implied, its implied form being "it", referring to the calf; إليهم is attached to يرجع and قولا is the mafʿūl bihi. For this reason the verb after it is nominative.
(وَلَقَدْ قالَ لَهُمْ هارُونُ مِنْ قَبْلُ): The wāw is a conjunction; the lām is the lām that paves the way for the oath (al-lām al-muwaṭṭiʾa li-l-qasam); قد is a particle of affirmation; قال لهم هارون is a past verb and its fāʿil; من قبل is attached to an omitted ḥāl, i.e. before the return of Moses.
(يا قَوْمِ إِنَّما فُتِنْتُمْ بِهِ وَإِنَّ رَبَّكُمُ الرَّحْمنُ فَاتَّبِعُونِي وَأَطِيعُوا أَمْرِي): يا is a vocative particle and قوم is a vocative (munādā) annexed to the omitted yāʾ of the first person; إنما is [إنّ] restrained and [ما] the restraining particle (kāffa wa-makfūfa); فتنتم is a passive past verb; the tāʾ is the nāʾib fāʿil and the mīm is the sign of the masculine plural; به is attached to فتنتم. وإن ربكم الرحمن: إنّ, its ism and its khabar. The fāʾ is the fāʾ al-faṣīḥa; اتبعوني is an imperative verb, indeclinable (mabnī) on the dropping of the nūn; the wāw is the fāʿil, the nūn is for protection (al-wiqāya) and the yāʾ is the mafʿūl bihi; أطيعوا أمري is conjoined to اتبعوني.
(قالُوا لَنْ نَبْرَحَ عَلَيْهِ عاكِفِينَ حَتَّى يَرْجِعَ إِلَيْنا مُوسى): لن is a particle of negation, of the accusative and of the future; نبرح is a defective (nāqiṣ) imperfect verb in the accusative (manṣūb) by لن; its ism is a latent pronoun, its implied form being "we"; عليه is attached to عاكفين, and عاكفين is the khabar of نبرح. حتى is a particle of limit and of the genitive; يرجع is an imperfect verb in the accusative by an implied أن after حتى; إلينا is attached to يرجع and موسى is the fāʿil. This suspension which they made the limit of their devotion was nothing [Translator's note: printed «أم يكن», evidently for «لم يكن»] on their part but procrastination and excuse-making; it is not of the nature of a promise to abandon its worship after the return of Moses.
(قالَ يا هارُونُ ما مَنَعَكَ إِذْ رَأَيْتَهُمْ ضَلُّوا): ما is an interrogative noun in the position of nominative as mubtadaʾ, and the clause منعك is the khabar; إذ is an adverb attached to منعك, and the clause رأيتهم is annexed to the adverb; رأيتهم is a verb, its fāʿil and its mafʿūl bihi; the clause ضلوا is circumstantial, or the second mafʿūl bihi of رأيتهم if you regard it as a verb of the heart (mental perception).
(أَلَّا تَتَّبِعَنِ أَفَعَصَيْتَ أَمْرِي): أن is a maṣdar-forming particle that puts into the accusative, and لا is redundant (mazīda), i.e. "what thing prevented you from following me in anger for Allah's sake? Why did you not fight those who disbelieved with those who believed?" The hamza is for the interrogative of disapproval; the fāʾ conjoins to something implied; عصيت is a past verb and its fāʿil, and أمري is the mafʿūl bihi.
(قالَ يَا بْنَ أُمَّ لا تَأْخُذْ بِلِحْيَتِي وَلا بِرَأْسِي): يا ابن أم: يا is a vocative particle; ابن and أم are two nouns indeclinable on fatḥa because they are compounded like the compounding of numbers such as خمسة عشر, or of adverbs such as صباح مساء. On this view ابن is not annexed to أم but is compounded with it, so their vowelling is the vowelling of indeclinability. The details of this construction were given in «al-Aʿrāf». In any case, they are in the position of accusative as a vocative. He confined himself in addressing him to the mother, although he was his full brother, because mentioning the mother is more softening of his heart. لا is prohibitive and تأخذ is an imperfect verb in the jussive (majzūm) by the prohibitive لا, its fāʿil latent, its implied form being "you"; بلحيتي is attached to تأخذ, and ولا برأسي is conjoined to بلحيتي. It is said that Moses was by nature given to sharpness and to anger for Allah and His religion, so when he saw his people worshipping other than Allah he could not restrain himself from seizing his brother's head and the hair of his face, dragging him towards himself.
(إِنِّي خَشِيتُ أَنْ تَقُولَ فَرَّقْتَ بَيْنَ بَنِي إِسْرائِيلَ وَلَمْ تَرْقُبْ قَوْلِي): إنّ and its ism; the clause خشيت is the khabar of إنّ; أن and what is within its scope are the object of خشيت; the clause فرقت is the object of the saying (maqūl al-qawl); بين is an adverb of place attached to فرقت, and بني إسرائيل is muḍāf ilayhi; ولم ترقب قولي is conjoined to فرقت, i.e. "and I feared that you would say: you did not observe my word"; on this view the pronoun in قولي refers to Moses. It is also permissible to conjoin it to خشيت, in which case the pronoun in قولي refers to Aaron.
(قالَ فَما خَطْبُكَ يا سامِرِيُّ): قال is a past verb whose fāʿil is latent, its implied form being "he", referring to Moses; the fāʾ is a conjunction or resumptive; ما is interrogative, a mubtadaʾ, and خطبك is the khabar; يا is a vocative particle and سامري is a single proper-name vocative (munādā mufrad ʿalam).
(قالَ بَصُرْتُ بِما لَمْ يَبْصُرُوا بِهِ فَقَبَضْتُ قَبْضَةً مِنْ أَثَرِ الرَّسُولِ): The clause بصرت is the object of the saying, and the fāʿil of قال is "he", i.e. al-Sāmirī; بما is attached to بصرت, and the clause لم يبصروا به is the ṣila (relative clause). فقبضت is conjoined to بصرت; قبضة is the mafʿūl bihi; it is the maṣdar of a single instance (maṣdar al-marra) of قبض, and applying it to the thing taken is calling the object by the maṣdar. من أثر is a naʿt of قبضة; أثر is muḍāf and الرسول is muḍāf ilayhi, on the implication of two omitted words, i.e. "from the track of the hoof of the horse of the messenger", the meaning being "from the earth where it trod". The details of the story are in the lengthy works, and we shall summarise for you what they said in the section on Rhetoric.
(فَنَبَذْتُها وَكَذلِكَ سَوَّلَتْ لِي نَفْسِي): فنبذتها is conjoined to قبضت, i.e. I threw it; كذلك is a naʿt of an omitted maṣdar, as has been given; سولت لي نفسي is a verb and its fāʿil, i.e. my soul made it seem fair to me.
(قالَ فَاذْهَبْ فَإِنَّ لَكَ فِي الْحَياةِ أَنْ تَقُولَ لا مِساسَ): قال is a past verb whose fāʿil refers to Moses. فاذهب: the fāʾ is a conjunction and اذهب is an imperative verb whose fāʿil is "you". فإن: the fāʾ is a conjunction [Translator's note: as printed; it is commonly parsed as causal]; إنّ is a particle resembling the verb; لك is its fronted khabar; في الحياة is attached to an omitted ḥāl; أن and what follows it are the ism of إنّ. لا is the lā of generic negation and مساس is the ism of لا, with the khabar omitted; it is indeclinable together with the generic لا. What is meant by it is prohibition, i.e. "do not touch me and I shall not touch you". مساس is the maṣdar of ماسّ, like قتال, the maṣdar of قاتل. Al-Zamakhsharī said: «He was punished in this world with a punishment than which nothing is more grievous or more desolate: namely that he was forbidden entirely from mixing with people, and it was forbidden to them to meet him, speak to him, trade with him, face him, and everything by which people live with one another. And if it happened that he touched anyone, man or woman, both the toucher and the touched would be seized with fever; so he avoided people and they avoided him».
(وَإِنَّ لَكَ مَوْعِداً لَنْ تُخْلَفَهُ): إنّ is a particle resembling the verb; لك is its fronted khabar and موعدا is its postponed ism; لن is a particle of negation, of the accusative and of the future; تخلفه is accusative by لن; the nāʾib fāʿil is latent, its implied form being "you", and the hāʾ is the second mafʿūl bihi.
(وَانْظُرْ إِلى إِلهِكَ الَّذِي ظَلْتَ عَلَيْهِ عاكِفاً لَنُحَرِّقَنَّهُ ثُمَّ لَنَنْسِفَنَّهُ فِي الْيَمِّ نَسْفاً): وانظر: the wāw is a conjunction and انظر is an imperative verb whose fāʿil is latent, its implied form being "you"; إلى إلهك is attached to انظر; الذي is a naʿt, and the clause ظلت is the ṣila. ظلت is a defective past verb; its origin is ظللت, with two lāms, the first of which, with kasra, was dropped for lightness. عليه is attached to عاكفا, and عاكفا is the khabar of ظلت. لنحرقنه: the lām paves the way for the oath; نحرقنه is an imperfect verb, indeclinable on fatḥa because it is attached to the nūn of emphasis; the fāʿil is latent, its implied form being "we", and the hāʾ is the mafʿūl bihi. ثم is a conjunction; لننسفنه is like نحرقنه; في اليم is attached to ننسفنه, and نسفا is a mafʿūl muṭlaq (absolute object).
(إِنَّما إِلهُكُمُ اللَّهُ الَّذِي لا إِلهَ إِلَّا هُوَ وَسِعَ كُلَّ شَيْءٍ عِلْماً): إنما is [إنّ] restrained and [ما] the restraining particle; إلهكم is a mubtadaʾ and الله is its khabar; the clause is resumptive (mustaʾnafa). الذي is a naʿt, and the clause لا إله إلا هو is the ṣila — its parsing has often been given. وسع is a past verb whose fāʿil is latent, its implied form being "He"; كل is the mafʿūl bihi [Translator's note: the source prints «وكل شيء مضاف اليه», omitting the parsing of كل; كل is the mafʿūl bihi and شيء is muḍāf ilayhi]; علما is a tamyīz (specification) converted from the fāʿil of وسع.

* Rhetoric:
The concision (al-ījāz) in these verses is very clear, and it is in every one of them, because the sequence of events requires the implying of clauses which are indispensable. We have pointed to them with clear indications that make repeating them unnecessary. But here we cite a concision by omission which occurs in the saying of the Exalted «فَقَبَضْتُ قَبْضَةً مِنْ أَثَرِ الرَّسُولِ»: the muḍāf has been omitted twice over here, the implied form being "from the track of the hoof of the horse of the messenger". This omission is very common in the Quran, as in the saying of the Exalted «وَلكِنَّ الْبِرَّ مَنِ اتَّقى», and His saying «حَتَّى إِذا فُتِحَتْ يَأْجُوجُ وَمَأْجُوجُ وَهُمْ مِنْ كُلِّ حَدَبٍ يَنْسِلُونَ», where the muḍāf of يأجوج ومأجوج, namely their barrier, has been omitted, just as the muḍāf of القرية has been omitted in the saying of the Exalted: «وَسْئَلِ الْقَرْيَةَ», i.e. the people of the town. It also occurs in poetry; of what has come of it is the saying of al-Khuzaymī lamenting Abū al-Hindām, and he is one of the poets of the Ḥamāsa:
إذا لاقيت قومي فاسأليهم ... كفى قوما بصاحبهم خبيرا
(When you meet my people, ask them — a people suffice as knowers of their companion:)
هل أعفو عن أصول الحق فيهم ... إذا عسرت وأقتطع الصدورا
(Do I not pardon the principal dues owed me among them when they are hard pressed, and cut away [the rancour of] the breasts?)
He meant that he cuts away the rancour that is in the breasts, i.e. he removes that by his kindness, of pardon and other things; so he omitted the muḍāf and put the muḍāf ilayhi in its place. Omission of the muḍāf is more frequent than omission of the muḍāf ilayhi. Of what has come in the Noble Quran of omission of the muḍāf ilayhi is the saying of the Exalted «لِلَّهِ الْأَمْرُ مِنْ قَبْلُ وَمِنْ بَعْدُ», i.e. before the victory and after it.
Summary of the story of al-Sāmirī:
We shall now go outside the scope which we have marked out for ourselves in this book — the scope of i'rab, language and eloquence — and cite a fleeting glimpse of the story of al-Sāmirī, because of its connection with what we are dealing with, leaving the reader room to refer to the lengthy works.
At the time when the appointed time for going to al-Ṭūr arrived, Allah sent Gabriel to Moses riding Ḥayzūm, the horse of life, to take him. Al-Sāmirī saw him and said: "This has some significance", and he took a handful from the track of the earth where it trod. When Moses asked him about his story, he said: "I took from the track of the horse of the one sent to you on the day the appointed time arrived" — and perhaps he did not know that he was Gabriel. It is said that whenever the horse placed its hoof on anything it turned green, so he knew that the earth on which the horse placed its hoof had some significance. Other things are said which the soul does not feel at ease with and which need much scrutiny.

* Benefits:
The one to whom the ḥāl refers (ṣāḥib al-ḥāl):
The basic rule for ṣāḥib al-ḥāl is definiteness, because it is that about which the ḥāl makes a judgement, and that about which a judgement is made should properly be definite, since a judgement about the unknown generally conveys nothing. Ṣāḥib al-ḥāl occurs as indefinite with a justification (musawwigh) that brings it close to the definite, in the following places:
1- When the ḥāl precedes it, e.g. «في الدار جالسا رجل», and the saying of Kuthayyir ʿAzza:
لمية موحشا طلل ... يلوح كأنه خلل
(Mayya has a desolate ruin, which gleams as if it were [faded] scabbard-linings.)
In al-Mughnī: putting the ḥāl of an indefinite noun before it is not in order to justify the ḥāl in it, but so that the ḥāl will not be confused with the naʿt.
2- That its ṣāḥib is particularised by a description, as in the poet's saying:
نجيت يا رب نوحا واستجبت له ... في فلك ماخر في اليم مشحونا
(You saved Noah, O Lord, and answered him, in a ship cleaving the sea, laden.)
So مشحونا is a ḥāl of فلك because it is described by ماخر.
3- That its ṣāḥib is particularised by annexation, as in the saying of the Exalted «فِي أَرْبَعَةِ أَيَّامٍ سَواءً لِلسَّائِلِينَ»; سواء is a ḥāl of أربعة because it is particularised by annexation to أيام.
4- That its ṣāḥib is particularised by something it governs, e.g. «عجبت من ضرب أخوك شديدا»; شديدا is a ḥāl of ضرب because it is particularised by governing the fāʿil, namely أخوك.
