5- That its ṣāḥib is particularised by conjunction, e.g. «هؤلاء أناس وعبد الله منطلقين»; منطلقين is a ḥāl of أناس because it is particularised by what is conjoined to it, namely عبد الله.
6- That its ṣāḥib is preceded by a negation, as in the saying of the Exalted «وَما أَهْلَكْنا مِنْ قَرْيَةٍ إِلَّا وَلَها كِتابٌ مَعْلُومٌ»; the clause ولها كتاب معلوم is a ḥāl of قرية because it is preceded by negation. It has been mentioned that al-Zamakhsharī rejects this view and makes the clause a naʿt of قرية, the wāw coming between them only to emphasise the attachment of the description to the thing described.
7- That its ṣāḥib is preceded by a prohibition, as in the saying of al-Ṭirimmāḥ:
لا يركنن أحد إلى الاحجام ... يوم الوغى متخوفا لحمام
(Let no one incline to holding back on the day of battle, fearing death.)
So متخوفا is a ḥāl of أحد because it is preceded by prohibition.
8- That its ṣāḥib is preceded by an interrogation, as in the saying of one of the poets of Ṭayyiʾ [Translator's note: printed «الطائبين», evidently for «الطائيين»]:
يا صاح هل حم عيش باقيا فترى ... لنفسك العذر في إبعادها الأملا
(O friend, has a lasting life been decreed, so that you see an excuse for yourself in its stretching hope far?)
So باقيا is a ḥāl of عيش because it is preceded by the interrogative هل. صاح is a vocative with truncation (murakhkham) of صاحب, irregularly; حم, with the unpointed ḥāʾ, means "decreed"; al-ibʿād is the maṣdar of أبعد, and الأمل is its object.
Ṣāḥib al-ḥāl may also occur as indefinite without a justification, as in their saying «عليه مائة بيضا»: بيضا, in the plural form, is a ḥāl of مائة and not a tamyīz — contrary to al-Mubarrad — because the tamyīz of مائة is never an accusative plural nor a genitive plural; and it is one of Sībawayh's examples. And in the ḥadīth: «The Messenger of Allah ﷺ prayed sitting, and behind him men standing (قياما)»; قياما is a ḥāl of رجال, which is indefinite without a justification.

dervis-irab:36-40.t:
* Vocabulary:
(السؤل): the request; it is of the pattern فُعْل in the sense of مفعول, like الخبز in the sense of المخبوز (what is baked) and الأكل in the sense of المأكول (what is eaten).
(التَّابُوتِ): a wooden chest.
(الْيَمِّ): the sea; by it is meant the river Nile.

* I'rab:
(قالَ قَدْ أُوتِيتَ سُؤْلَكَ يا مُوسى): the clause قد أوتيت is the object of the saying (maqūl al-qawl); أوتيت is a passive past verb, the tāʾ is the nāʾib fāʿil (deputy agent), and سؤلك is the second object of أوتيت.
(وَلَقَدْ مَنَنَّا عَلَيْكَ مَرَّةً أُخْرى): the wāw is resumptive (istiʾnāfiyya); the lām is the answer to an omitted oath; قد is a particle of realization (taḥqīq); مننا is a verb and its fāʿil (agent); عليك is attached to (mutaʿalliq) مننا; مرة is an adverb or a mafʿūl muṭlaq (absolute object); and أخرى is an adjective of مرة.
(إِذْ أَوْحَيْنا إِلى أُمِّكَ ما يُوحى): إذ is an adverb that here conveys cause (taʿlīl), and it is attached to مننا; the clause أوحينا is what the adverb is annexed to; إلى أمك is attached to أوحينا. ما is maṣdariyya, interpreted together with what follows it as a maṣdar (verbal noun) which is a mafʿūl muṭlaq; or it is a relative, in which case it is the nāʾib fāʿil [Translator's note: so in the source; as a relative, ما would be the object of أوحينا, and the nāʾib fāʿil of يوحى is the pronoun referring to it], and the clause يوحى is the ṣila (relative clause). It conveys ibhām (vagueness), which will come in the section on Rhetoric.
(أَنِ اقْذِفِيهِ فِي التَّابُوتِ فَاقْذِفِيهِ فِي الْيَمِّ): أن is explicative (mufassira), because revelation (الوحي) is in the sense of saying; اقذفيه is an imperative verb, its agent and its mafʿūl bihi (direct object); في التابوت is attached to اقذفيه; فاقذفيه في اليم is conjoined to اقذفيه في التابوت. The pronouns do not differ, because the one cast is Moses, peace be upon him.
(فَلْيُلْقِهِ الْيَمُّ بِالسَّاحِلِ يَأْخُذْهُ عَدُوٌّ لِي وَعَدُوٌّ لَهُ): the fāʾ is a conjunction; the lām is the lām of command; يلقه is an imperfect verb in the jussive (majzūm) by the lām of command, the sign of its jussive being the dropping of the weak letter; the hāʾ is a direct object; and اليم is the agent. This is a command whose meaning is a statement; and because it is a command in wording, its answer in His saying يأخذه is jussive. Further explanation of it will come in the section on Rhetoric. بالساحل is attached to يلقه, or to an omitted ḥāl (circumstantial), i.e. "being in contact with it". يأخذه is the answer to the command (jawāb al-ṭalab); the hāʾ is the object; عدو is the agent; لي is an adjective; and عدو له is conjoined to عدو لي.
(وَأَلْقَيْتُ عَلَيْكَ مَحَبَّةً مِنِّي وَلِتُصْنَعَ عَلى عَيْنِي): the wāw is a conjunction; ألقيت is a verb and its agent; عليك is attached to ألقيت; محبة is a direct object; and مني is an adjective of محبة, i.e. a great love coming from Me — so, inevitably, everyone who saw you loved you. It is also possible to attach مني to ألقيت. ولتصنع is conjoined to an implied reason understood from the context of the speech, i.e. "so that you might be loved by people". لتصنع: the lām is for cause (taʿlīl), and تصنع is a passive imperfect verb in the accusative (manṣūb) by an implied أن after the lām; على عيني is a ḥāl, i.e. so that you might be brought up and treated well while I watch over you, observe you and guard you. The discussion of the majāz mursal (metonymic trope) here will come in the section on Rhetoric.
(إِذْ تَمْشِي أُخْتُكَ فَتَقُولُ هَلْ أَدُلُّكُمْ عَلى مَنْ يَكْفُلُهُ؟): إذ is an adverb of cause attached to ألقيت, or to تصنع, or to an omitted element, its implied form being اذكر ("remember"). The clause تمشي is what the adverb is annexed to; أختك is the agent; تقول is conjoined to تمشي; هل is an interrogative particle; أدلكم is an imperfect verb whose agent is latent (mustatir), its implied form being "I", and the kāf is a direct object; على من is attached to أدلكم; and the clause يكفله is the ṣila.
(فَرَجَعْناكَ إِلى أُمِّكَ كَيْ تَقَرَّ عَيْنُها وَلا تَحْزَنَ): the fāʾ conjoins to something omitted for conciseness, its implied form being "so her request was granted, his mother came, and Moses accepted her breast".
رجعناك is a verb, its agent and its object; إلى أمك is attached to رجعناك; كي is an accusative-governing particle; تقر is accusative by كي; عينها is the agent; and ولا تحزن is conjoined to كي تقر.
(وَقَتَلْتَ نَفْساً فَنَجَّيْناكَ مِنَ الْغَمِّ وَفَتَنَّاكَ فُتُوناً): قتلت is a verb and its agent, and نفسا is the object of قتل. Moses killed the Copt in Egypt; his name was Qāb Qān [Translator's note: so in the source], and he was a cook of Pharaoh; Moses's age at that time was thirty years. فنجيناك: the fāʾ is a conjunction; نجيناك is a verb, its agent and its object; من الغم is attached to نجيناك. فتناك is a verb, its agent and its object; فتونا is a mafʿūl muṭlaq if it is a maṣdar — and this is the more likely — like القعود, الجلوس, الشكور, الثبور and اللزوم; or it is accusative by removal of the preposition (manṣūb bi-nazʿ al-khāfiḍ) if it is the plural of فتنة, i.e. "with various kinds of trials". The meaning is: We tested you and tried you with various kinds of hardship.
(فَلَبِثْتَ سِنِينَ فِي أَهْلِ مَدْيَنَ ثُمَّ جِئْتَ عَلى قَدَرٍ يا مُوسى): the fāʾ is a conjunction; لبثت is a verb and its agent; سنين is an adverb of time attached to لبثت. It was said that he stayed with the prophet Shuʿayb in Midian for ten years, during which he married his daughter; and it was said twenty-eight years, of which the dowry of his daughter was ten years, since he completed the longer of the two terms. في أهل مدين is attached to لبثت; مدين is annexed to أهل, a diptote because it is a proper name and feminine. ثم is a conjunction; جئت is a verb and its agent; على قدر is a ḥāl, i.e. in accordance with what was decreed for you, or settled at a fixed measure; and يا موسى is a vocative. Jarīr borrowed this construction in his saying in praise of ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz:
أتى الخلافة أو كانت له قدرا ... كما أتى ربه موسى على قدر
(He came to the caliphate, or it was decreed for him, just as Moses came to his Lord according to a decree.)

* Rhetoric:
The rhetorical devices of these verses are very many; we present the most important of them below:

1- Explanation after vagueness (al-tafsīr baʿd al-ibhām):
The first is explanation after vagueness. This kind is used to magnify and aggrandize the matter left vague, because it strikes the hearing after [the mind] has been attached to something vague; so the faculties sway, and the hearer's mind goes in every direction. In this manner came the saying of the Exalted «قالَ قَدْ أُوتِيتَ سُؤْلَكَ يا مُوسى، وَلَقَدْ مَنَنَّا عَلَيْكَ مَرَّةً أُخْرى»: He made the speech vague and brought it in summary form so that the mind would be engaged and look out [wondering]: what might the request be? What is the other favour? And what favours and blessings might follow it?
It longs for knowledge and tries to grasp the reality; then His saying comes after that, explaining what was made vague, and He says «إذ أوحينا إلى أمك ما يوحى أن اقذفيه في التابوت فاقذفيه في اليم». If you ask: what is the first favour? What is the second favour?
And are there further favours after that? I say: the total of the favours that Allah bestowed on His prophet Moses is eight:
a- His saying «إذ أوحينا» up to His saying «وعدو له».
b- His saying «وألقيت عليك محبة مني», etc.
c- His saying «ولتصنع على عيني» up to His saying «من يكفله».
d- His saying «فرجعناك إلى أمك» up to His saying «ولا تحزن».
e- His saying «وقتلت نفسا فنجيناك من الغم».
[f-] His saying «وفتناك فتونا».
g- His saying «فلبثت في أهل مدين» up to His saying «يا موسى».
h- His saying «واصنعتك لنفسي» [Translator's note: so in the source; the Quranic wording, in the next verse (20:41), is «وَاصْطَنَعْتُكَ لِنَفْسِي»].

2- Vagueness (al-ibhām):
As for pure vagueness, it is His saying «ما يوحى»; it is very common in the Noble Quran. Its like in poetry is the saying of Durayd ibn al-Ṣimma in elegy for his brother:
صبا ما صبا حتى علا الشيب رأسه ... فلما علاه قال للباطل: ابعد
(He indulged in youthful folly as he did, until grey hair rose upon his head; when it had risen upon it, he said to frivolity: "Be gone!")
More delightful examples of it will come.

3- The rational trope (al-majāz al-ʿaqlī):
The majāz ʿaqlī is in the saying of the Exalted «فَلْيُلْقِهِ الْيَمُّ بِالسَّاحِلِ»: He ascribed the casting to the sea (اليم), which has no reason; but it represents the will of Allah and His intention, which does not err and from which nothing escapes. The bringing [to the shore], decreed in the world of the Unseen and the realm of the divine will, is ascribed to it as though it possessed discernment, obeying the command and complying with its prescription.

4- Indefiniteness (al-tankīr):
He made المحبة indefinite and ascribed it to Himself, Glorified, for two important reasons: 1- the intrinsic grandeur in indefiniteness, as though it were a love surpassing the customary love exchanged between creatures.
2- the relational grandeur in ascribing it to Himself, i.e. a great love from Me, which I have planted in hearts and fixed in the innermost selves and the folds of consciences. So glory be to the Speaker of these words.

5- The metonymic trope (al-majāz al-mursal):
In His saying «على عيني» there is a majāz mursal: by "the eye" He meant love, i.e. "on love from Me", because the eye is its forerunner and its cause; so the relationship is causality (al-sababiyya). Abū ʿUbayda and Ibn al-Anbārī said: the meaning is "that you may be nourished upon My love and My will"; you say "I take things on my eye", i.e. on my love. Ibn al-Anbārī said: "the eye" in this verse is meant in the sense of will and choice, from the Arabs' saying "so-and-so is on my eye", i.e. [he enjoys] love from me. It was said that the lām is attached to something omitted, i.e. "I did that so that you might be made"; and it was said it is attached to ألقيت.

dervis-irab:99-104.t:
* Vocabulary:
(وِزْراً): a heavy load; what is meant by it here is the heavy, oppressive, crushing punishment. He called it a wizr, likening it, in its heaviness upon the one on whom the punishment falls, to a heavy load under which the shoulders bend and the bearer staggers beneath its grievous weight.
(زُرْقاً): plural of azraq [Translator's note: printed «أرزق»]. The reason for choosing it for their eyes on [the Day of] Resurrection is twofold:
1- Blueness was the most hateful of the colours of eyes to the Arabs [Translator's note: printed «العيوب» (faults), evidently for «العيون» (eyes)], because the Byzantines were their enemies and they were blue-eyed. Among their sayings in describing the enemy: «black of liver, reddish of moustache, blue of eye». أصهب is from al-ṣuhba, with the unpointed ṣād, which is a redness or fairness in the hair; al-sibāl is the hair on the moustache and the front of the beard, and both are meant here. Bashshār said in describing the miser:
وللبخيل على أمواله علل ... زرق العيون عليها أوجه سود
(The miser has pretexts over his wealth — blue-eyed [hostile] ones, with black faces upon them.)
It is from delightful verses which we cite in full:
ظل اليسار على العباس ممدود ... وقلبه أبدا بالبخل معقود
(The shade of wealth is spread over al-ʿAbbās, yet his heart is ever bound up in miserliness.)
إن الكريم ليخفي عنك عسرته ... حتى تراه غنيا وهو مجهود
(The generous man hides his hardship from you, so that you see him as rich while he is exhausted.)
وللبخيل على أمواله علل ... زرق العيون عليها أوجه سود
(The miser has pretexts over his wealth — blue-eyed ones, with black faces upon them.)
إذا تكرهت أن تعطي القليل ولم ... تقدر على سعة لم يظهر الجود
(If you are loath to give little and cannot give amply, generosity will not appear.)
أورق بخير ترجّي للنوال فما ... ترجى الثمار إذا لم يورق العود
(Put forth leaves of good, so that you may be hoped for gifts; fruit is not hoped for when the branch does not leaf.)
بثّ النوال ولا تمنعك قلته ... فكل ما سدّ فقرا فهو محمود
(Spread your gifts, and let not their smallness hold you back, for whatever stops a need is praiseworthy.)
2- What is meant is blindness, because the pupil of one whose sight has gone turns bluish.
(يَتَخافَتُونَ بَيْنَهُمْ): i.e. they lower their voices and hide them, because of the terror and horror that has befallen them. In al-Mukhtār: «خفت الصوت: the voice became still; it is of the pattern jalasa. Al-mukhāfata, al-takhāfut and al-khaft, on the pattern of al-sabt: speaking secretly».
(أَمْثَلُهُمْ): the best of them and most upright in opinion or deed in the life of this world. Its plural is amāthil and muthul, and its feminine is muthlā. Amāthil al-qawm are the best of the people; al-ṭarīqa al-muthlā is the one most resembling the truth. One says «المريض اليوم أمثل», i.e. in a better state. Imruʾ al-Qays said, describing the night, in his Muʿallaqa:
وليل كموج البحر أرخى سدوله ... عليّ بأنواع الهموم ليبتلي
(Many a night like the waves of the sea has let down its curtains upon me with all kinds of cares, to try me.)
فقلت له لما تمطى بصلبه ... وأردف إعجازا وناء بكلكل
(I said to it, when it stretched out its back, made its hindquarters follow and rose heavily with its breast:)
ألا أيها الليل الطويل ألا انجلي ... بصبح وما الإصباح منك بأمثل
(O long night, will you not clear away into morning? — though the morning is no better than you.)

* I'rab:
(كَذلِكَ نَقُصُّ عَلَيْكَ مِنْ أَنْباءِ ما قَدْ سَبَقَ وَقَدْ آتَيْناكَ مِنْ لَدُنَّا ذِكْراً): كذلك is a naʿt (adjective) of an omitted maṣdar (verbal noun), i.e. "just as We have related to you, O Muḥammad, this story". نقص is an imperfect verb whose fāʿil (agent) is latent (mustatir), its implied form being "We"; عليك is a preposition and its genitive noun attached to (mutaʿalliq) نقص; من أنباء is a naʿt of an omitted noun described, which is the mafʿūl bihi (direct object) of نقصّ, i.e. "We relate a report from among the reports"; ما is muḍāf ilayhi, and the clause قد سبق is the ṣila (relative clause). وقد: the wāw is a conjunction and قد is a particle of affirmation; آتيناك is a past verb, its fāʿil and its mafʿūl bihi; من لدنا is a ḥāl (circumstantial), because it was [originally] a naʿt of ذكرا; ذكرا is the second mafʿūl bihi, i.e. a Quran.
(مَنْ أَعْرَضَ عَنْهُ فَإِنَّهُ يَحْمِلُ يَوْمَ الْقِيامَةِ وِزْراً): من is conditional, in the position of nominative as mubtadaʾ (subject); أعرض is a past verb in the position of jussive as the protasis (fiʿl al-sharṭ), its fāʿil a latent pronoun, its implied form being "he"; عنه is attached to أعرض; the fāʾ is linking; إنّ and its ism, and the clause يحمل is its khabar (predicate), its fāʿil latent, its implied form being "he"; يوم القيامة is an adverb attached to يحمل, and وزرا is the object. The clause من أعرض is in the position of accusative as a naʿt of ذكرا, i.e. a Quran comprising and containing these stories, the one who turns away from which will bear a full burden on the Day of Resurrection.
(خالِدِينَ فِيهِ وَساءَ لَهُمْ يَوْمَ الْقِيامَةِ حِمْلًا): خالدين is a ḥāl and فيه is attached to خالدين; the pronoun refers to the burden, i.e. in the punishment caused by it, so there is a trope in the speech, as will come. وساء: the wāw is circumstantial or a conjunction; ساء is a past verb, one of the verbs of blame — it has often been given — and its fāʿil is latent, specified by an indefinite noun, namely حملا; the one specifically blamed (al-makhṣūṣ bi-l-dhamm) is omitted, its implied form being "their burden". لهم is attached to an implied saying, i.e. "these words are said to them"; it is also said that it is like the lām in «هيت لك», i.e. merely for clarification; so refer to Sūrat Yūsuf. يوم القيامة is an adverb attached to ساء, and حملا is a tamyīz (specification).
(يَوْمَ يُنْفَخُ فِي الصُّورِ وَنَحْشُرُ الْمُجْرِمِينَ يَوْمَئِذٍ زُرْقاً): The adverb is a badal (substitute) from يوم القيامة; the clause ينفخ is annexed to the adverb; ينفخ is an imperfect verb in the passive, and في الصور is attached to ينفخ. ونحشر: the wāw is a conjunction; نحشر is an imperfect verb whose fāʿil is latent, its implied form being "We"; المجرمين is the mafʿūl bihi; يوم is an adverb annexed to an adverb like it, attached to نحشر; the tanwīn on إذ is in compensation for a clause; زرقا is a ḥāl of المجرمين.
(يَتَخافَتُونَ بَيْنَهُمْ إِنْ لَبِثْتُمْ إِلَّا عَشْراً): The clause is a ḥāl of المجرمين, or resumptive (mustaʾnafa), brought to explain their state on that day. يتخافتون is an imperfect verb in the nominative (marfūʿ) by the retention of the nūn, because it is one of the five verbs, and the wāw is the fāʿil; بينهم is an adverb attached to يتخافتون. The clause إن لبثتم is in the accusative by a saying indicated by يتخافتون, and the saying is accusative as a ḥāl, i.e. "saying in secret". إن is negative; لبثتم is a verb and its fāʿil; إلا is a particle of restriction (ḥaṣr); عشرا is an adverb of time, taking it to refer to nights, because the beginnings of months are nights, so the days are included as following. Their whispering stems from the terror that has entered them, so that it is as though the days of this world had been nothing worth mentioning; they recall the days of joy that came their way in this world, how they passed over them like the shadow of a bird in flight.
(نَحْنُ أَعْلَمُ بِما يَقُولُونَ إِذْ يَقُولُ أَمْثَلُهُمْ طَرِيقَةً إِنْ لَبِثْتُمْ إِلَّا يَوْماً): نحن is a mubtadaʾ and أعلم is the khabar; بما is attached to أعلم, and the clause يقولون is the ṣila; إذ is an adverb attached to أعلم, and the clause يقول is annexed to the adverb; أمثلهم is the fāʿil and طريقة is a tamyīz; إن is negative; لبثتم is a verb and its fāʿil; إلا is a particle of restriction, and يوما is an adverb attached to لبثتم.

* Rhetoric:
Al-majāz al-mursal (non-metaphorical trope) in His saying «خالِدِينَ فِيهِ», i.e. in the burden. One does not abide in a burden; rather He meant the punishment caused by the burden, so the relation in it is causality.

dervis-irab:41-47.t:
* Vocabulary:
(وَاصْطَنَعْتُكَ): I chose you for Myself from among all people. Further discussion of the figurative usage (majāz) in this graceful expression will come.
(تَنِيا): [i.e.] do not slacken. الونى is slackness and falling short; one says ونى يني ونيا, like وعد يعد وعدا, when one slackens; the noun is الونى, which is slackness. ونى is an intransitive verb that does not take an object. Some grammarians claimed that it can be one of the sisters of زال and انفك, and so operate as they do, on condition of negation; one says ما ونى زيد قائما, i.e. ما زال زيد قائما ("Zayd did not cease standing"). In al-Miṣbāḥ:
"ونى في الأمر ونيا, of the تعب and وعد patterns: he was weak and slackened, so he is وان; in the Revelation «ولا تنيا في ذكري». توانى في الأمر توانيا: he did not hasten to take it in hand and paid no attention to it, so he is متوان, i.e. not concerned and not caring." In the verse it is of the وعد pattern, because of the kasra on the nūn; had it been of the تعب pattern, it would have had fatḥa. In al-Asās he alluded to the possibility of this verb operating like لا يزال; he said: "لا يني يفعل: he does not cease doing; امرأة وناة: a woman in whom there is languor." In al-Qāmūs:
"الونى, like الفتى, is fatigue and slackness — [a word of] opposite [meanings] — and it may be lengthened; ونى يني ونيا وونيا ووناء وونية ونية وونى; he caused him to slacken (أوناه); he slackened (توانى); ناقة وانية: a languid, exhausted she-camel; امرأة وناة, أناة and إنية: a forbearing woman, slow in standing, sitting and walking; الميناء: the harbour of a ship, and it may be lengthened, and the substance of glass [i.e. enamel]; الونية, like اللؤلؤة, like الوناة: a pearl, or a necklace of pearls."
(يَفْرُطَ): one says فرط يفرط, of the قعد pattern, علينا فلان, when someone hastens [to us] with something hateful.

* I'rab:
(وَاصْطَنَعْتُكَ لِنَفْسِي): a past verb, its fāʿil (agent) and its mafʿūl bihi (direct object); لنفسي is attached to (mutaʿalliq) it.
(اذْهَبْ أَنْتَ وَأَخُوكَ بِآياتِي وَلا تَنِيا فِي ذِكْرِي): اذهب is an imperative verb whose agent is latent (mustatir), its implied form being "you"; أنت is a detached pronoun, a tawkīd (emphasis) of the latent pronoun. The clause is resumptive (mustaʾnafa), brought to establish what is meant by "choosing". أخوك is conjoined to the nominative pronoun, the sign of its nominative being the wāw, and the kāf is the muḍāf ilayhi (genitive construct). بآياتي is a ḥāl (circumstantial), because the bāʾ is for accompaniment (muṣāḥaba), i.e. accompanied by My signs and holding fast to them; it is not for making [the verb] transitive, because what is meant is displaying the signs to people, not merely going to Pharaoh. The wāw is a conjunction; لا is prohibitive; تنيا is an imperfect verb in the jussive (majzūm) by prohibitive لا, and the alif is the agent; في ذكري is attached to تنيا. It was said that في here means عن, i.e. "[do not slacken] from My worship" — but I have not seen it attributed to anyone, so it is better that it keep its literal sense of containment (ẓarfiyya), as though [the remembrance] contained the falling short. However, he said in al-Mughnī: "What appears is that the meaning of ونى عن كذا is that he passed beyond it and did not enter into it, and ونى فيه is that he entered into it and slackened." This favours that it is for containment, not for passing beyond.
(اذْهَبا إِلى فِرْعَوْنَ إِنَّهُ طَغى): اذهبا is a verb and its agent; إلى فرعون is attached to اذهبا; إن and its noun, and the clause طغى is its khabar (predicate).
(فَقُولا لَهُ قَوْلًا لَيِّناً لَعَلَّهُ يَتَذَكَّرُ أَوْ يَخْشى): the fāʾ is a conjunction; قولا is an imperative verb and its agent; له is attached to قولا; قولا is a mafʿūl muṭlaq (absolute object) and لينا an adjective. لعل and its noun, and the clause يتذكر is its khabar; أو is a conjunction, and يخشى is conjoined to يتذكر. The meaning of hope (tarajjī) here and in general will come in the section on Benefits.
(قالا رَبَّنا إِنَّنا نَخافُ أَنْ يَفْرُطَ عَلَيْنا أَوْ أَنْ يَطْغى): قالا is a past verb and its agent; ربنا is an annexed vocative; إن and its noun, and the clause نخاف is its khabar; أن and what falls within its scope is the object of نخاف; علينا is attached to يفرط; أو is a conjunction, and أن يطغى is conjoined to أن يفرط.
(قالَ لا تَخافا إِنَّنِي مَعَكُما أَسْمَعُ وَأَرى): لا is prohibitive; تخافا is an imperfect verb in the jussive by لا, and the alif is the agent; the clause لا تخافا is the object of the saying (maqūl al-qawl). The clause إنني معكما gives the reason for not fearing; إن and its noun, and the adverb is attached to an omitted khabar; the clause أسمع is a second khabar or a ḥāl; and أرى is conjoined to أسمع.
(فَأْتِياهُ فَقُولا إِنَّا رَسُولا رَبِّكَ): فأتياه: the fāʾ is the faṣīḥa (the fāʾ indicating an implied condition), and أتياه is an imperative verb, its agent and its object; فقولا is conjoined to فأتياه; إن and its noun, رسولا is its khabar, and ربك is the muḍāf ilayhi.
(فَأَرْسِلْ مَعَنا بَنِي إِسْرائِيلَ وَلا تُعَذِّبْهُمْ): the fāʾ is also the faṣīḥa; أرسل is an imperative verb whose agent is latent, its implied form being "you"; معنا is an adverb of place attached to أرسل; بني إسرائيل is a direct object. ولا تعذبهم: لا is prohibitive, تعذبهم is jussive by لا, and the hāʾ is a direct object.
(قَدْ جِئْناكَ بِآيَةٍ مِنْ رَبِّكَ وَالسَّلامُ عَلى مَنِ اتَّبَعَ الْهُدى): the clause قد جئناك is a ḥāl; it functions, relative to the clause إنا رسولا ربك, as clarification and explanation, because a claim to messengership is not established unless supported by signs and manifest proofs indicating it. قد is a particle of realization (taḥqīq); جئناك is a past verb, its agent and its object; بآية is attached to جئناك; من ربك is an adjective of آية. The wāw is resumptive; السلام is a mubtadaʾ (subject); and على من اتبع الهدى is the khabar.

* Benefits:
The linguists and grammarians have paid attention to the meaning of hope (al-rajāʾ) in the saying of the Exalted «لَعَلَّهُ يَتَذَكَّرُ أَوْ يَخْشى». We shall summarize the aspects they mentioned, because there is not room to cite them in their own words. The hope may bear the following [interpretations]:
1- That the hope here is in its proper sense, with respect to those sent, namely Moses and Aaron, i.e. "go, holding your hope for his faith, and undertake the matter as one who hopes and longs for his work to bear fruit, so that he exhausts his effort and expends all he can". It is impossible for that to apply to Allah the Exalted, since He knows the outcomes and what is hidden. It is reported from Sībawayh: "Every لعل and عسى occurring in the Quran is, from Allah, a certainty." This is explicit that hope cannot possibly retain its meaning with respect to Allah the Exalted.
2- That لعل conveys cause (taʿlīl), so it is equivalent to كي; this is the view of al-Farrāʾ. He said:
as you say "Work, لعلك you take your wage", i.e. so that (كي) you take your wage.
3- That it is interrogative, i.e. "will he remember and fear?" This view is rejected, because interrogation is impossible with respect to Allah the Exalted.

What the grammarians say:
The grammarians say that لعل is for expectation (al-tawaqquʿ). Some expressed this as hope (al-tarajjī) for something desired, as in "Perhaps the beloved is coming", and from it is the saying of the Exalted «لَعَلَّ اللَّهَ يُحْدِثُ بَعْدَ ذلِكَ أَمْراً»; and apprehension (al-ishfāq) about something disliked, as in «فلعلك باخع نفسك», i.e. killing yourself — the meaning being: I fear for you that you will kill yourself from grief at missing the Islam of your people; its discussion has preceded. الإشفاق in the language is fear: one says أشفقت عليه in the sense of "I feared for him", and أشفقت منه in the sense of "I feared him and was wary of him".
al-Akhfash and al-Kisāʾī said: لعل also comes for cause, as in what a man says to his companion: "Finish your work, لعلنا we have lunch", and "Do your work, لعلك you take your wage", i.e. so that we have lunch and so that you take [it]. From it is «لعله يتذكر», i.e. so that he may remember. He said in al-Mughnī: whoever does not affirm that interprets it as hope and directs it to the two addressees, i.e. "go, holding your hope".

dervis-irab:105-114.t:
* Vocabulary:
(قاعاً): al-qāʿ is smooth, low-lying land from which the mountains and hillocks have parted; the plural is aqwāʿ, aqwuʿ, qīʿ, qīʿān and qīʿa. It is also said to be the exposed part of the earth; and it is said to be the level, hard part of it; and it is said to be that in which there is neither plant nor building.
(صَفْصَفاً): al-ṣafṣaf is level, smooth land, as if its parts were a single row (ṣaff) from every side. In al-Qāmūs: the level part of the earth; «قاع صفصف»: level and low-lying. So it is in the status of a tawkīd (emphasis) of القاع, because it has its meaning.
(أَمْتاً): al-amt is a slight protrusion; one says «مدّ حبله حتى ما فيه أمت» (he stretched his rope until there was no slack in it). It is also said that al-amt is the hillock, which is close to the first; and it is said to be cracks in the ground; and it is said to be hillocks. In al-Qāmūs: «أمته يأمته: he estimated it and assessed it, like أمّته, and he aimed at it; أجل مأموت: a fixed term; al-amt: an elevated place, small hills, depression and elevation, and unevenness in a thing — the plural is amāt and umūt — and weakness and feebleness, and the good way, and crookedness, and a defect in the mouth, in a garment and in stone, and that one place should be thick and another thin; al-muʾammat: the filled, and one suspected of evil and the like; and "wine has been forbidden — لا أمت فيها", i.e. there is no doubt about its prohibition».
(هَمْساً): al-hams is a hidden sound; it is the maṣdar (verbal noun) of «همست الكلام», of the pattern ḍaraba, when you concealed it; from it are the voiceless letters (al-ḥurūf al-mahmūsa). It is also said to be from hams al-ibil, which is the sound of the camels' pads when they walk.
(وَعَنَتِ): In al-Mukhtār: «عنا يعنو, of the pattern سما يسمو سموّا» — the alif is dropped before the tāʾ of the feminine because of the meeting of two sukūns — when he was humbled and submitted; from it is al-ʿunāt, plural of ʿānin, which is the captive.
(هَضْماً): al-haḍm is diminution. The Arabs say: «هضمت لزيد من حقه», i.e. I diminished part of it. From it is «هضيم الكشحين», i.e. slender of flanks. Imruʾ al-Qays said:
إذا قلت هاتي نوليني تمايلت ... عليّ هضيم الكشح ريا المخلخل
(When I said, "Come, grant me your favour", she leaned towards me, slender of waist, full where the anklet sits.)
«رجل هضيم» and «مهتضم» mean wronged; هضمته, اهتضمته and تهضمته all have one meaning.

* I'rab:
(وَيَسْئَلُونَكَ عَنِ الْجِبالِ فَقُلْ يَنْسِفُها رَبِّي نَسْفاً): The wāw is for resumption, and the clause is resumptive (mustaʾnafa), brought to establish their obstinacy and their persistence in disputation, arrogant denial and mockery. يسألونك is an imperfect verb in the nominative (marfūʿ) by the retention of the nūn; the wāw is the fāʿil (agent) and the kāf is the mafʿūl bihi (direct object). فقل: the fāʾ is a conjunction and قل is an imperative verb whose fāʿil is latent (mustatir), its implied form being "you"; the clause ينسفها is the object of the saying (maqūl al-qawl); the hāʾ is a fronted mafʿūl bihi and ربي is a postponed fāʿil; نسفا is a mafʿūl muṭlaq (absolute object).
(فَيَذَرُها قاعاً صَفْصَفاً): The fāʾ is a conjunction; يذرها is an imperfect verb whose fāʿil is latent, its implied form being "He", i.e. Allah the Exalted; the hāʾ is the mafʿūl bihi. قاعا: you may parse it as a ḥāl (circumstantial) of the accusative pronoun, or as a second mafʿūl bihi because يذر is made to include the sense of "making into" (al-taṣyīr). صفصفا is a second ḥāl, or a badal (substitute) from the second object; some parsed it as a naʿt (adjective) of it.
(لا تَرى فِيها عِوَجاً وَلا أَمْتاً): The clause is a third ḥāl, or a first ḥāl [Translator's note: i.e. depending on whether قاعا and صفصفا are parsed as ḥāls]. لا is negative; ترى is an imperfect verb whose fāʿil is latent, its implied form being "you"; فيها is a preposition and its genitive noun attached to (mutaʿalliq) ترى; عوجا is the mafʿūl bihi, and ولا أمتا is conjoined. Further explanation of this verse will come in the section on Rhetoric.
(يَوْمَئِذٍ يَتَّبِعُونَ الدَّاعِيَ لا عِوَجَ لَهُ): The adverb is attached to يتبعون, or is a badal from the يوم القيامة mentioned earlier; the explanation of annexing يوم to the adverb [إذ] has been given. يتبعون الداعي is an imperfect verb, its fāʿil and its mafʿūl bihi; لا is the lā of generic negation; عوج is its ism, indeclinable (mabnī) on fatḥa, and له is its khabar (predicate). The clause لا عوج له is a ḥāl of الداعي, or a naʿt of an omitted maṣdar, i.e. "they follow him with a following that has no crookedness"; it may also be resumptive. The first is more evident, because the pronoun in له refers to him, i.e. there is no crookedness in his call; rather all of them hear it, and he does not incline to some people rather than others.
(وَخَشَعَتِ الْأَصْواتُ لِلرَّحْمنِ فَلا تَسْمَعُ إِلَّا هَمْساً): The wāw is a conjunction; خشعت الأصوات is a verb and its fāʿil; للرحمن is attached to خشعت; the fāʾ is a conjunction and لا is negative; تسمع is an imperfect verb whose fāʿil is latent, its implied form being "he" [Translator's note: as printed; the address is to "you"]; إلا is a particle of restriction (ḥaṣr), and همسا is the mafʿūl bihi, because the exception is emptied (mufarragh).
(يَوْمَئِذٍ لا تَنْفَعُ الشَّفاعَةُ إِلَّا مَنْ أَذِنَ لَهُ الرَّحْمنُ وَرَضِيَ لَهُ قَوْلًا): The adverb is attached to تنفع, and إذ is muḍāf ilayhi [Translator's note: printed «مضاف»]. لا is negative; تنفع الشفاعة is an imperfect verb and its fāʿil; إلا is a particle of restriction. As for من, it may be the object of تنفع, in which case من refers to the one interceded for; or it may be a badal from الشفاعة, according to the rule for the excepted in a negative statement; or accusative as a connected exception (istithnāʾ muttaṣil) from الشفاعة. In these two options a muḍāf must be implied, its implied form being "except the intercession of one to whom He has given permission". If it is regarded as a disconnected exception, it must be accusative. So there result four options of nearly equal weight. Al-Zamakhsharī preferred the nominative as a badal, and the Qāḍī al-Bayḍāwī followed him.
The clause أذن له الرحمن is the ṣila (relative clause), and رضي له قولا is conjoined to أذن له. Abū al-Baqāʾ preferred the accusative as an object.
(يَعْلَمُ ما بَيْنَ أَيْدِيهِمْ وَما خَلْفَهُمْ وَلا يُحِيطُونَ بِهِ عِلْماً): The clause is resumptive, brought to establish His knowledge, the Exalted, of the states which preceded them and of what lies ahead of them. يعلم is an imperfect verb in the nominative whose fāʿil is latent, its implied form being "He"; ما is the mafʿūl bihi; بين is an adverb attached to an omitted ṣila of the relative noun, and أيديهم is annexed to بين; وما خلفهم is conjoined to ما بين أيديهم. ولا يحيطون: you may make the wāw a conjunction and you may make it circumstantial; يحيطون is an imperfect verb in the nominative by the retention of the nūn; به is attached to يحيطون, and علما is the mafʿūl bihi [Translator's note: as printed; it is more commonly parsed as tamyīz].
(وَعَنَتِ الْوُجُوهُ لِلْحَيِّ الْقَيُّومِ وَقَدْ خابَ مَنْ حَمَلَ ظُلْماً): وعنت الوجوه is a verb and its fāʿil; للحي is attached to عنت, and القيوم is a naʿt. What is meant by «the faces» will come in the section on Rhetoric [Translator's note: it does not appear in this entry's Rhetoric section]. The wāw is circumstantial, and the clause وقد خاب is circumstantial; من is the fāʿil of خاب, and the clause حمل ظلما is the ṣila.
(وَمَنْ يَعْمَلْ مِنَ الصَّالِحاتِ وَهُوَ مُؤْمِنٌ فَلا يَخافُ ظُلْماً وَلا هَضْماً): The wāw conjoins to وقد خاب; من is conditional, a mubtadaʾ (subject); يعمل is the protasis (fiʿl al-sharṭ); من الصالحات is a naʿt of an omitted mafʿūl bihi, i.e. "whoever does deeds among the righteous ones". The wāw is circumstantial; هو is a mubtadaʾ and مؤمن is the khabar. The fāʾ links the apodosis (jawāb al-sharṭ); لا is negative; يخاف is an imperfect verb whose fāʿil is latent, its implied form being "he"; ظلما is the mafʿūl bihi and ولا هضما is conjoined to ظلما. The clause لا يخاف is the khabar of an omitted mubtadaʾ, the implied form being "then he does not fear"; the clause فهو لا يخاف is in the position of jussive as the apodosis, and the protasis and its apodosis are the khabar of من.
(وَكَذلِكَ أَنْزَلْناهُ قُرْآناً عَرَبِيًّا): The kāf is a naʿt of an omitted maṣdar, i.e. "like that sending down We sent it down"; قرآنا is a ḥāl and عربيا is a naʿt.
(وَصَرَّفْنا فِيهِ مِنَ الْوَعِيدِ لَعَلَّهُمْ يَتَّقُونَ أَوْ يُحْدِثُ لَهُمْ ذِكْراً): صرفنا is a verb and its fāʿil; فيه is attached to صرفنا; من الوعيد is a naʿt of an omitted object, i.e. "We have varied a threat among the threats". لعلّ and its ism, and the clause يتقون is its khabar; أو is a conjunction and يحدث is conjoined to يتقون; لهم is attached to يحدث, and ذكرا is the mafʿūl bihi; the fāʿil of يحدث is "it", i.e. the Quran.
(فَتَعالَى اللَّهُ الْمَلِكُ الْحَقُّ وَلا تَعْجَلْ بِالْقُرْآنِ مِنْ قَبْلِ أَنْ يُقْضى إِلَيْكَ وَحْيُهُ وَقُلْ رَبِّ زِدْنِي عِلْماً): The fāʾ is resumptive; تعالى الله is a past verb and its fāʿil; الملك and الحق are two naʿts of الله. ولا تعجل: the wāw is a conjunction and لا is prohibitive; تعجل is an imperfect verb in the jussive (majzūm) by the prohibitive لا; بالقرآن is attached to تعجل, and من قبل is attached to تعجل; أن يقضى: the interpreted maṣdar is muḍāf ilayhi to قبل; إليك is attached to يقضى; يقضى is a passive imperfect verb, and وحيه is the nāʾib fāʿil (deputy agent). وقل is conjoined to لا تعجل; رب is a vocative (munādā) annexed to the omitted yāʾ of the first person; زدني is an imperative verb, the nūn is for protection (al-wiqāya) and the yāʾ is the first mafʿūl bihi; علما is the second mafʿūl bihi or a tamyīz (specification).

* Rhetoric:
In the saying of the Exalted «لا تَرى فِيها عِوَجاً وَلا أَمْتاً» there is a charming device which astonishes the mind and intoxicates the feelings, and which hardly anyone grasps except those in whom Allah has deposited the secret of eloquence (bayān) and who have trained themselves through toil and practice in grasping the subtle points that are hard and long for whoever seeks them. This device they called the device of «al-tankīt» (pointed choice). Its definition is that the speaker singles out something for mention to the exclusion of anything else that would take its place, and of what the outward sense of the speech would require, because of a subtle point (nukta) in what is mentioned which gives its coming preference over anything else. It is frequent in the Noble Quran and will come in its places. As for this verse: it was given in al-Kahf that the lexicographers distinguished between ʿiwaj and ʿawaj, saying: ʿiwaj with kasra is in abstract things, and ʿawaj with fatḥa is in concrete things; that is why He said in al-Kahf «الحمد لله الذي أنزل الكتاب ولم يجعل له عوجا». But in this verse the earth is a concrete thing, so how is it correct to use with it the form with kasra on the ʿayn? Does not what the language requires make it necessary to use ʿawaj with fatḥa? Here this device comes to sound the depth of this subtle point, which is too fine for the first, superficial glance and does not stop at the lexical rulings. So we say:
The choice of ʿiwaj with kasra in the verse has a fine and marvellous place in the levelness of the earth, its description as smooth and the negation of crookedness from it in the most eloquent manner. For if you set about a piece of land and levelled it, and went to great lengths in levelling it to your eye and to the eyes of those expert in lands, and you all agreed unanimously that no crookedness at all remained in it, and then you went to the surveyor to seek his opinion — not according to guesswork, conjecture and bare looking, but according to the geometric measurements built on exact science — he would find crookedness in it in more than one place. That is not perceived by the sense of sight but by geometric measurement, which does not go astray and from which the rare small thing does not escape.
So Allah, Glorified is He, negated that crookedness which is too fine and subtle for perception and understanding — except, O Allah, by the measurement which the one versed in estimation and geometry knows. Since that crookedness is not perceived except by measurement and not by sensation, and has joined the abstract things and risen above the concrete ones, ʿiwaj with kasra was said of it.
There have already been with us, and there will be in this book, splendid examples of this tankīt which has appeared to you in this noble verse, of the kind only inspired experts perceive. So let us postpone speaking about them; and now we shall present before your eyes examples of beautiful poetry containing an ingenious subtle point, so that they may be for you landmarks of daybreak to follow. Of that is the saying of al-Khansāʾ lamenting her brother Ṣakhr:
يذكرني طلوع الشمس صخرا ... وأذكره لكل غروب شمس
(The rising of the sun reminds me of Ṣakhr, and I remember him at every setting of the sun.)
Al-Aṣmaʿī was asked about this saying of hers: why did she single out in it the rising and setting of the sun, rather than the middle of the day? He said: because the rising of the sun is the time of riding out to raids, and the setting of the sun is the time of entertaining guests.
And of it is the saying of al-Ḥasan ibn Hāniʾ, Abū Nuwās:
ألا فاسقني خمرا وقل لي هي الخمر ... ولا تسقني سرا إذا أمكن الجهر
(Come, give me wine to drink and tell me, "It is wine"; and do not give it to me in secret when openness is possible.)
He said «وقل لي هي الخمر» because four senses had taken pleasure when he drank it, and one sense remained which had not had its full pleasure, namely the sense of hearing; so he said «وقل لي هي الخمر» so that he might hear that, and his pleasure would be complete with all his senses.
We shall be content now with what has preceded, and we shall return to this beautiful device.

dervis-irab:48-55.t:
* I'rab:
(إِنَّا قَدْ أُوحِيَ إِلَيْنا أَنَّ الْعَذابَ عَلى مَنْ كَذَّبَ وَتَوَلَّى): إن and its noun, and the clause قد أوحي is the khabar (predicate); إلينا is attached to (mutaʿalliq) أوحي; أن and what falls within its scope is interpreted as a maṣdar (verbal noun) which is the nāʾib fāʿil (deputy agent) of أوحي; أن and its noun, and على من is its khabar; the clause كذب is the ṣila (relative clause); and تولى is conjoined to كذب.
(قالَ فَمَنْ رَبُّكُما يا مُوسى): i.e. so they came to him and said all that was mentioned. So the fāʾ conjoins to something implied; من is an interrogative noun, the mubtadaʾ (subject); ربكما is the khabar; and the clause is the object of the saying (maqūl al-qawl). Aaron is not mentioned [in the address] because he was a follower, a support and a vizier to him. Other things were said that are of no use.
(قالَ رَبُّنَا الَّذِي أَعْطى كُلَّ شَيْءٍ خَلْقَهُ ثُمَّ هَدى):
ربنا is a mubtadaʾ and الذي its khabar; the clause أعطى is the ṣila; كل شيء is the first object and خلقه the second object. It was also said that خلقه is the first of the two objects of أعطى and كل شيء the second, placed first for emphasis, i.e. He gave His creation (خليقته) — "which is the plural of الخلائق" [Translator's note: so in the source; الخلائق is in fact the plural of خليقة] — everything they need. It was also read خَلَقَه, as a verb, the second object being omitted because it is known. ثم هدى is conjoined to أعطى, i.e. He gave each thing its form and cast it in the skin suited to the properties and uses entrusted to it, and guided each creature to that for which it was created. On this concision there is lengthy discussion, which the reader will find in the section on Rhetoric.
(قالَ فَما بالُ الْقُرُونِ الْأُولى): the fāʾ is a conjunction; ما is interrogative, the mubtadaʾ; بال is the khabar; القرون is the muḍāf ilayhi (genitive construct); and الأولى is an adjective.
(قالَ عِلْمُها عِنْدَ رَبِّي فِي كِتابٍ لا يَضِلُّ رَبِّي وَلا يَنْسى): علمها is a mubtadaʾ; the adverb عند ربي is attached to an omitted khabar, and في كتاب is a ḥāl (circumstantial); or في كتاب is the khabar and عند ربي a ḥāl; or both are khabars; or both together are a single khabar, as in your saying "the pomegranate is sweet-sour", i.e. tart. The clause لا يضل is resumptive (mustaʾnafa); it was also said to be an adjective of كتاب, the returning pronoun being omitted, its implied form being "in a book which my Lord does not lose", or "whose keeping my Lord does not lose". ربي is the agent of يضل, and لا ينسى is conjoined to لا يضل. What the scholars said about the meaning of this verse will come in the section on Benefits.
(الَّذِي جَعَلَ لَكُمُ الْأَرْضَ مَهْداً وَسَلَكَ لَكُمْ فِيها سُبُلًا): الذي is the khabar of an omitted mubtadaʾ, i.e. هو; the clause جعل is the ṣila; لكم is a ḥāl, because it was [originally] an adjective of مهادا [Translator's note: the source uses the reading مهادا throughout here, while the verse as quoted reads مهدا]; الأرض is the first object and مهادا the second. سلك is a past verb whose agent is latent (mustatir), its implied form being "He"; لكم is attached to an omitted ḥāl, because it was [originally] an adjective of سبلا; فيها is attached to سلك; and سبلا is a mafʿūl bihi (direct object).
(وَأَنْزَلَ مِنَ السَّماءِ ماءً فَأَخْرَجْنا بِهِ أَزْواجاً مِنْ نَباتٍ شَتَّى): أنزل is conjoined to what precedes; من السماء is attached to أنزل; ماء is a direct object. فأخرجنا: the fāʾ is a conjunction; أخرجنا is a verb and its agent; به is attached to أخرجنا; أزواجا is a direct object; من نبات is an adjective of أزواجا; and شتى is an adjective of أزواجا, or a ḥāl of it because it has been qualified. al-Zamakhsharī allowed it to be an adjective of النبات.
(كُلُوا وَارْعَوْا أَنْعامَكُمْ إِنَّ فِي ذلِكَ لَآياتٍ لِأُولِي النُّهى): كلوا is an imperative verb and its agent, and the clause is governed by an omitted ḥāl, i.e. "saying", or "permitting the use of them, allowing you to eat some of them and to feed some to your animals". ارعوا is conjoined to كلوا, and أنعامكم is the object of ارعوا. إن is a particle resembling the verb; في ذلك is the fronted khabar of إن; لآيات: the lām is the shifted lām (al-lām al-muzaḥlaqa), and آيات is the postponed noun of إن; لأولي النهى is an adjective of آيات; النهى is the muḍāf ilayhi of أولي, and it is the plural of نُهية; it was also said to be a singular noun.
(مِنْها خَلَقْناكُمْ وَفِيها نُعِيدُكُمْ وَمِنْها نُخْرِجُكُمْ تارَةً أُخْرى): منها is attached to خلقناكم; فيها is attached to نعيدكم; منها is attached to نخرجكم; تارة is an adverb attached to نخرجكم; and أخرى is an adjective of تارة.

* Rhetoric:
1- Concision (al-ījāz):
In the saying of the Exalted «ثُمَّ هَدى» there is an eloquent concision, because it omits clauses beyond counting: it is not possible to count the living and non-living, rational and non-rational creatures that Allah has created, each of which has its work made easy for it, in accordance with his saying ﷺ: «كل ميسر لما خلق له» ("Each is facilitated for what he was created for"). So it is difficult — indeed impossible — for anyone to speak about the general utilities and the giving of each utility to its owner, created for it, who knows how to make use of what he was given and how to reach it. For this reason al-Zamakhsharī spoke well when he said: "How excellent is this answer! How concise it is, how comprehensive, and how clear to one who pays attention, looks with the eye of fairness and seeks the truth!" Further, the concision has another benefit: Pharaoh, after Moses, peace be upon him, had nearly exposed him and refuted his superstitions, wished to divert him to matters of no concern to him, unconnected with the message — tales and legends. Moses answered him that this is not among the particular concerns of the message, but rather "its knowledge is with my Lord". So when he asked him about his Lord, he made his speech concise in this marvellous way.

2- Iltifāt (shift of person):
From the third person to the first person, in reporting the speech of Allah, Mighty and Majestic. Its benefit is to draw attention to how evident is what is in the earth of indication of the perfection of the divine power, of wisdom that does not go astray, and of the submission of all creatures to His will. It was also said that there is no iltifāt in the speech, because it is a condition of iltifāt that it be in the speech of a single speaker who turns his speech in various ways, and what we have here is not of that kind. For Allah the Exalted related from Moses, peace be upon him, his saying to Pharaoh «علمها عند ربي في كتاب لا يضل ربي ولا ينسى», and then his saying «الذي جعل لكم الأرض مهادا» up to His saying «فأخرجنا به أزواجا من نبات شتى». Either it is made part of the speech of Moses — in which case it is like the saying of the king's intimates, "we commanded" and "we built", by which they mean the king, and this is not iltifāt; or Moses's speech ended at his saying «ولا ينسى», and then Allah the Exalted began describing Himself with the attributes of His favours to His creation — so it is not iltifāt either, but a transition from reporting to initiating an address.
This reply may seem sound at first glance; but we note that Moses described Allah the Exalted with these attributes in the third person, saying: "Who made the earth a cradle for you, threaded paths for you in it, sent down water from the sky, and brought forth (فأخرج) with it pairs of diverse plants". When Allah the Exalted reported it from him, He ascribed the pronoun to Himself, because the one reporting is the one referred to in Moses's speech; so the referent of the two pronouns is the same. This aspect is subtle, and it is the aspect closest to iltifāt.

* Benefits:
On «لا يضل ربي ولا ينسى»:
The most fitting thing that can be said about negating error and forgetfulness of Allah the Exalted — when He has no need of such negation, since He is the Knower of the unseen — is that it is a form of taʿrīḍ (indirect allusion). The meaning is: everything that exists is encompassed by His knowledge and recorded with Him in a book, and error and forgetfulness are not possible for Him as they are possible for you, O abased slave and puny human — i.e. He does not go astray as you go astray, O claimant to lordship, through ignorance, arrogance and insolence.
al-Qaffāl said: "There is a difference between يضل and ينسى, i.e. He does not go astray from things and from knowing them, and what He knows of that He does not forget. So the first word indicates His being knowing of all knowables, and the second word is proof of the permanence of that knowledge for ever and ever; it is an indication of the negation of change."
There is disagreement about the meaning of «لا يضل ربي ولا ينسى», on several views:
The first: that it is the beginning of a new statement declaring Allah the Exalted free of these two attributes, the sentence having been completed at His saying «في كتاب».
The second: that the meaning of لا يضل is "He does not err".
The third: that its meaning is "nothing is absent [from Him]".
The fourth: that its meaning is that He does not need a book; knowledge of nothing among things escapes Him, and He does not forget what He knows of them.
The fifth: that these two clauses are an adjective of كتاب, and the meaning is that the book does not go away from Allah, nor does He forget it.

dervis-irab:115-123.t:
* Vocabulary:
(تَضْحى): the heat of the sun befalls you in the forenoon. In al-Qāmūs: «ضحا يضحو, like غزا يغزو, ḍaḥwan: he was exposed to the sun; and like سعى and رضي, ḍaḥwan and ḍuḥiyyan: the sun struck him».
(وسوس): the whispering (waswasa) of Satan is like the wailing (walwala) of the bereaved woman and the howling (waʿwaʿa) of the wolf, in that they are imitations of sounds. We shall speak about the names of sounds and their imitations in the section on Benefits. It came in al-Qāmūs: «وسوس, waswāsan and waswasatan: Satan whispered to him and towards him; he spoke to him of evil or of what has no benefit and no good. وسوس الرجل: the man was afflicted in his mind and spoke without order, and whisperings afflicted him, so he is muwaswas; and he spoke hidden speech. Al-waswās: the sound of jewellery. وسوس الرجل: he spoke to him with hidden speech. وسوس به, in the passive: his speech became confused and he was bewildered. Al-waswās is the noun from وسوس; al-waswās is Satan; al-waswās is a disease which arises from the predominance of black bile and with which the mind becomes confused. Whatever occurs to the heart of evil, or of what has no good, is called waswās, and its plural is wasāwis».
(سَوْآتُهُما): their private parts; this has been given before.
(يَخْصِفانِ): i.e. they stick together; from خصف النعل, which is to sew strips (khiṣāf) onto the sandal; i.e. they stick the leaves of the trees one onto another until it becomes broad and suitable for covering.
(اجْتَباهُ): He chose him and brought him near; from «جبى إليّ كذا فاجتبيته» (such-and-such was collected to me, so I gathered it up). So al-mujtabā is, as it were, in origin the one in whom good qualities have been gathered, so that another chooses him.

* I'rab:
(وَلَقَدْ عَهِدْنا إِلى آدَمَ مِنْ قَبْلُ فَنَسِيَ وَلَمْ نَجِدْ لَهُ عَزْماً): A resumptive (mustaʾnafa) clause, brought to establish the evils of forgetfulness, which is the twin of ignorance and its companion; for that reason one must guard against it and always pray with the saying of the Exalted «وَقُلْ رَبِّ زِدْنِي عِلْماً». The lām is the response to the omitted oath; قد is a particle of affirmation; عهدنا is a verb and its fāʿil (agent); إلى آدم is a preposition and its genitive noun attached to (mutaʿalliq) عهدنا; من قبل is attached to an omitted ḥāl (circumstantial). فنسي is conjoined to عهد, i.e. he forgot what We had commanded him; i.e. forgetfulness is something ingrained in the nature of the children of Adam. ولم نجد: the wāw is a conjunction and لم is a particle of negation, inversion [of the tense] and the jussive; the fāʿil is latent (mustatir), its implied form being "We"; عزما is the mafʿūl bihi (direct object).
(وَإِذْ قُلْنا لِلْمَلائِكَةِ اسْجُدُوا لِآدَمَ فَسَجَدُوا إِلَّا إِبْلِيسَ أَبى): The adverb is attached to an implied «اذكر», i.e. "and remember the time of what befell Adam: the enmity of Iblīs, his whispering to him and his making eating from the tree seem fair to him, and Adam's hastening to obey him after the far-reaching advice and the warning against Satan, his cunning and his snares that had gone before". The parsing of the verse has often been given, so there is no need to repeat it; and do not forget the scholars' disagreement over whether the exception is connected or disconnected. The clause أبى is circumstantial.
(فَقُلْنا يا آدَمُ إِنَّ هذا عَدُوٌّ لَكَ وَلِزَوْجِكَ): The fāʾ is a conjunction; قلنا is a verb and its fāʿil; يا آدم is a vocative; the clause إنّ is the object of the saying (maqūl al-qawl); هذا is the ism of إنّ and عدو is its khabar (predicate); لك is a naʿt (adjective) of عدو, and لزوجك is conjoined to لك.
(فَلا يُخْرِجَنَّكُما مِنَ الْجَنَّةِ فَتَشْقى): The fāʾ is a conjunction and لا is prohibitive; يخرجنكما is an imperfect verb, indeclinable (mabnī) on fatḥa, in the position of jussive (majzūm) by لا; the kāf is the mafʿūl bihi and the fāʿil is latent, namely Iblīs; the mīm and the alif are for the dual. فتشقى: the fāʾ is the fāʾ of causation (fāʾ al-sababiyya); تشقى is an imperfect verb in the accusative (manṣūb) by an implied أن after the fāʾ of causation, its fāʿil latent, its implied form being "you". The verb of wretchedness is attributed to Adam alone because the wretchedness of his wife is bound up with his wretchedness, just as her happiness is bound up with his happiness; so the speech was abbreviated while preserving the verse-ending (fāṣila).
(إِنَّ لَكَ أَلَّا تَجُوعَ فِيها وَلا تَعْرى): إنّ is a particle resembling the verb; لك is a fronted khabar; أن and what is within its scope are its postponed ism; فيها is attached to تجوع, and ولا تعرى is conjoined to لا تجوع.
(وَأَنَّكَ لا تَظْمَؤُا فِيها وَلا تَضْحى): Conjoined to the one before it. Marvellous discussion about separating hunger from thirst and nakedness from exposure to the sun, and the rhetorical secret before which necks are cut short [in striving to reach it], will come in the section on Rhetoric. There remains a difficulty, namely the conjoining of أنك to أن لا تجوع, so that it is as if it were the ism of إنّ with kasra; and this is not allowed: one does not say «إن أن زيدا منطلق». But since there is a separation between them here, it is permissible; so you say «إن عندي أن زيدا قائم», where عندي is the khabar, put before the ism — which is أنّ and what is within its scope — because it is an adverb.
The verse is of this kind. Al-Zamakhsharī took another view and said: «If you say: إنّ does not enter upon أنّ, so one does not say "إن أن زيدا منطلق", and the wāw is a substitute for إنّ and stands in its place, so why has it been made to enter upon it? I say: the wāw was not coined so as always to be a substitute for إنّ; rather it is a substitute for every governor. So since it is not a particle coined specifically for affirmation like إنّ [Translator's note: printed «كأن», evidently for «كإنّ»], their combination is not prohibited as the combination of إنّ and أنّ is prohibited».
Ibn Hishām said, in the course of discussing the places in which the hamza of إنّ may take kasra or fatḥa: «The sixth: that it occurs after a wāw preceded by a single word (mufrad) suitable to be conjoined to, e.g. «إن لك أن لا تجوع فيها ولا تعرى وأنك لا تظمأ فيها ولا تضحى». Nāfiʿ and Abū Bakr read it with kasra in «وإنك لا تظمأ», either as resumption, in which case it is a clause cut off from what preceded it, or by conjunction to the first إنّ clause, namely «إن لك أن لا تجوع»; on both views it is a clause with no grammatical position. The rest of the Seven read it by conjunction to أن لا تجوع, as conjoining a single word to its like, the implied form being "you have the absence of hunger and the absence of thirst"».
(فَوَسْوَسَ إِلَيْهِ الشَّيْطانُ قالَ يا آدَمُ هَلْ أَدُلُّكَ عَلى شَجَرَةِ الْخُلْدِ وَمُلْكٍ لا يَبْلى): فوسوس: the fāʾ is a conjunction and وسوس is a past verb; إليه is attached to وسوس and الشيطان is the fāʿil. قال يا آدم: a past verb and a vocative; هل is an interrogative particle; أدلك is an imperfect verb whose fāʿil is latent, its implied form being "I", and the kāf is the mafʿūl bihi; على شجرة الخلد is attached to أدلك; ملك is conjoined to شجرة, and the clause لا يبلى is a naʿt of ملك.
(فَأَكَلا مِنْها فَبَدَتْ لَهُما سَوْآتُهُما وَطَفِقا يَخْصِفانِ عَلَيْهِما مِنْ وَرَقِ الْجَنَّةِ وَعَصى آدَمُ رَبَّهُ فَغَوى): أكلا is a past verb and the alif is the fāʿil; منها is attached to أكلا; فبدت is conjoined to أكلا; لهما is attached to بدت, and سوءاتهما is the fāʿil. طفقا is a past verb, one of the verbs of commencement which operate like كاد, with the khabar occurring as an imperfect verb; the alif is its ism, and the clause يخصفان is the khabar of طفقا; عليهما is attached to يخصفان; من ورق الجنة is a naʿt of an omitted noun described, which is the mafʿūl bihi, i.e. "leaves from the leaves of the Garden". It is said to be the fig; it is better that it be general so as to include all the leaves of the trees. عصى آدم ربه is a verb, its fāʿil and its mafʿūl bihi, and فغوى is conjoined to عصى.
(ثُمَّ اجْتَباهُ رَبُّهُ فَتابَ عَلَيْهِ وَهَدى): ثم is a conjunction; اجتباه is a verb and its object, and ربه is the fāʿil; فتاب عليه is conjoined to اجتباه, and هدى is conjoined to تاب.
(قالَ اهْبِطا مِنْها جَمِيعاً بَعْضُكُمْ لِبَعْضٍ عَدُوٌّ): اهبطا is an imperative verb, indeclinable on the dropping of the nūn, and the alif is the fāʿil; منها is attached to اهبطا; جميعا is a ḥāl; بعضكم is a mubtadaʾ (subject); لبعض is a ḥāl, because it was [originally] a naʿt of عدو; عدو is the khabar; the clause بعضكم لبعض عدو is in the position of accusative as a ḥāl.
(فَإِمَّا يَأْتِيَنَّكُمْ مِنِّي هُدىً فَمَنِ اتَّبَعَ هُدايَ فَلا يَضِلُّ وَلا يَشْقى): The fāʾ is a conjunction; إن is conditional and ما is redundant (zāʾida); يأتينكم is an imperfect verb, indeclinable on fatḥa, in the position of jussive as the protasis (fiʿl al-sharṭ); the kāf is the mafʿūl bihi; مني is attached to يأتينكم, and هدى is the fāʿil of يأتينكم. فمن اتبع: the fāʾ is linking; من is conditional, a mubtadaʾ; اتبع is a past verb in the position of jussive as the protasis; هداي is the mafʿūl bihi; the fāʾ links the apodosis, and the clause لا يضل is in the position of jussive as the apodosis (jawāb al-sharṭ); the protasis and its apodosis are the khabar of من, and the clause من اتبع is in the position of jussive as the apodosis of إن.

* Rhetoric:
In the saying of the Exalted «إِنَّ لَكَ أَلَّا تَجُوعَ فِيها وَلا تَعْرى، وَأَنَّكَ لا تَظْمَؤُا فِيها وَلا تَضْحى» there is a marvellous device called «cutting the counterpart off from its counterpart» (qaṭʿ al-naẓīr ʿan al-naẓīr). That is, He cut thirst off from hunger and exposure to the sun off from clothing, despite the correspondence between them. The purpose of this is to realise the enumeration of these blessings and their classification; had He joined each to its like, the things enumerated would have been imagined to be a single blessing. Some scholars of bayān call it «the device of al-tawhīm» (creating a false impression), and reference to it has already been made. It is that the speaker brings a word such that what comes after it in the speech gives the impression that the speaker intended a misreading (taṣḥīf) of it while he intends something else. Of it is that there comes in the outward speech something that gives the impression of a solecism departing from the language; of it is that whose outward form gives the impression that the speech has been turned from its proper way without benefit; and of it is what comes indicating that the outward speech is corrupt in meaning while it is sound.
This verse is of the type whose outward form gives the impression that the arrangement of the speech has come in a way other than the way of eloquence, because its wording is not harmonious with its meaning, owing to the lack of congruity you see in the words. But when the reflective person reflects on it as it deserves, he finds it running on the method of eloquence, such that had it come as the objector imagined, the arrangement would have been faulty. In the verse, the one with the false impression says: had it been said "you will not hunger, nor thirst, nor be exposed to the sun, nor be naked", that would have run according to the congruity which eloquence requires. The answer is that its coming as the one with the false impression imagined would spoil the meaning of the arrangement; because had it been said "you have that you will not hunger in it nor thirst", He would have had to say "and that you will not be naked in it nor be exposed to the sun" — and al-taḍaḥḥī is being exposed to the sun without cover. Al-Hudhalī said — and it is also said [to be by] al-Majnūn, as in the Amālī of al-Qālī:
سلبت عظامي لحمها فتركتها ... مجردة تضحى لديك وتخصر
(You stripped my bones of their flesh and left them bare, exposed to the sun before you and chilled.)
i.e. they meet the forenoon sun bare, so its heat afflicts them, and meet the cold of the night bare, so its cold afflicts them; so they are tormented night and day. And since al-taḍaḥḥī is being exposed to the sun without cover, its meaning would be nakedness, and the meaning of the speech would become: "and that you will not be naked in it nor be naked" — and this is an evident corruption. Since this corruption necessarily attaches to the arrangement in the way the one with the false impression imagined, it was necessary to turn away from it to the wording of the Quran, namely that He, Glorified is He, joined to the negation of hunger the negation of nakedness, so that the soul would be at ease with the stopping of hunger and the covering of the private parts, which the necessity of life calls for and human nature demands by its constitution. And since hunger is put before thirst, just as eating is put before drinking, eloquence required that the mention of thirst come after hunger and before exposure to the sun, because it is important, and the promise of its negation had to come first, just as the promise of the negation of hunger came first; and that the mention of exposure to the sun come later, just as the mention of nakedness came after hunger, because exposure to the sun is of the genus of nakedness and thirst is of the genus of hunger. If it is said: why did He mention exposure to the sun, which is nakedness in meaning, when the mention of nakedness would have sufficed? I say: in the mention of exposure to the sun there is a great benefit, namely describing the Garden as having no sun in it, as He, Glorified is He, said: «لا يَرَوْنَ فِيها شَمْساً وَلا زَمْهَرِيراً». For al-taḍaḥḥī is a particular nakedness, conditioned by exposure to the sun at the time of ḍuḥā (forenoon); that is why it is called taḍaḥḥī. And moving from the more general to the more particular is eloquence, because the more particular is distinguished by what is not found in the more general.
Al-ʿIzz ibn ʿAbd al-Salām said in al-Amālī: What would have been appropriate by way of majāz [Translator's note: as printed; the sense suggests "by way of matching (mujānasa)"] is "that you will not hunger, nor thirst, nor be naked, nor be exposed to the sun", so as to combine like with like; so why did He depart from this? The answer: in the verse there is a jinās (correspondence) better than this; namely that hunger is the inside being stripped of nourishment and nakedness is the outside being stripped of covering, so in the verse He made the two strippings correspond; and likewise thirst is the heat of the inside and al-ḍuḥā, which is appearing to the sun, is the heat of the outside, so He made them correspond by combining the two heats.
The masters of rhetoric, old and new, have aspired to the heights of this meaning. Abū al-Ṭayyib al-Mutanabbī said:
وقفت وما في الموت شك لواقف ... كأنك في جفن الردى وهو نائم
(You stood when, for one who stood there, there was no doubt of death — as if you were in the eyelid of destruction while it slept.)
تمرّ بك الأبطال كلمى هزيمة ... ووجهك وضّاح وثغرك باسم
(The heroes pass by you, wounded and routed, while your face is radiant and your mouth smiling.)
It is related that when Sayf al-Dawla asked him one day to recite his ode which begins:
على قدر أهل العزم تأتي العزائم ... وتأتي على قدر الكرام المكارم
(Resolves come in the measure of the people of resolve, and noble deeds come in the measure of the noble.)
and he reached these two verses, Sayf al-Dawla said: "I have criticised these two against you, just as Imruʾ al-Qays was criticised for his saying:
كأني لم أركب جوادا للذة ... ولم أتبطّن كاعبا ذات خلخال
(As if I had never ridden a steed for pleasure, nor embraced a full-breasted maiden wearing an anklet,)
ولم أسبأ الزق الروي ولم أقل ... لخيلي كرّي كرّة بعد إجفال
(nor bought the brimming wineskin, nor said to my horsemen, 'Charge again after the rout!')
For the two hemistichs of your two verses do not fit together, just as the two hemistichs of Imruʾ al-Qays's two verses did not fit together. You ought to have said:
وقفت وما في الموت شك لواقف ... ووجهك وضاح وثغرك باسم
(You stood when, for one who stood there, there was no doubt of death, while your face was radiant and your mouth smiling;)
تمر بك الأبطال كلمى هزيمة ... كأنك في جفن الردى وهو نائم
(The heroes pass by you, wounded and routed, as if you were in the eyelid of destruction while it slept.)"
Al-Mutanabbī said: "If it is true that the one who made this correction to Imruʾ al-Qays knows poetry better than he, then Imruʾ al-Qays erred and I have erred. But my lord knows that the cloth-merchant does not know the garment as the weaver knows it, because the cloth-merchant knows it as a whole, while the weaver knows its details. Imruʾ al-Qays joined women with the pleasure of riding for the hunt, and joined liberality in buying wine for guests with bravery in fighting enemies. Likewise, when I mentioned death at the beginning of the first verse, I followed it with the mention of destruction at its end, so that it would be more harmonious; and since the face of the wounded man in rout is frowning and his eye weeping, I said «ووجهك وضاح وثغرك باسم», so as to combine opposites."
Moreover, there is in this verse a secret for that, in addition to what has been mentioned, namely that the correspondence of the verse-endings (fawāṣil) was intended; had He joined thirst to hunger, the string of the verse-endings would have come apart — and how beautiful it is, well ordered!

* Benefits:
The names of sounds (asmāʾ al-aṣwāt):
We promised you a discussion of the names of sounds, and we think we should expand on them a little, because the books of grammar seldom attend to them. They run the course of the verbal nouns (asmāʾ al-afʿāl), because they are akin to them; they are indeclinable (mabnī), and they divide into two types:
a- That with which what is not rational is addressed, which resembles the verbal noun in being sufficient by itself; but the verbal noun is compound, while the name of a sound is single because it does not carry a pronoun. As in their saying, in calling camels to drink: «جىء جىء», with kasra on the jīm in both, repeated, with hamza. In al-Muḥkam: they are a command to the camels to come down to the water; one says «جأجأت الإبل» when you called them to drink and said «جىء جىء»; al-Jawharī transmitted it from al-Umawī. And as in their saying in calling sheep «حاحا» and in calling goats «عاعا», without hamza; the verb from them is حاحيت and عاعيت. Sībawayh said: they substituted the alif for the yāʾ because of its resemblance to it, because your saying حاحيت is only a sound from which you have built a verb, and it is not [of the pattern] fāʿaltu. And as in their saying in driving on the mule:
عدس ما لعباد عليك إمارة ... أمنت وهذا تحملين طليق
(Adas! ʿAbbād has no authority over you; you are safe, and this one you carry is set free.)
عدس is a sound by which the mule is driven on, and the mule may be named by it; the implied form, on naming it by it, is «يا عدس», with the vocative particle omitted. Imāra, with kasra on the hamza, means rule.
b- That by which a heard sound is imitated. That whose sound is imitated is of two kinds, animal and other: the first is like «غاق», with the pointed ghayn and the qāf, for the sound of the crow; the second is like «طاق», imitating the sound of striking, and «طق», with fatḥa on the ṭāʾ, imitating the sound of stones falling on one another. More discussion of the names of sounds will come in this book.

A selection of the names of sounds:
Below is a chosen group of the names of sounds:
al-ṣarīr: the sound of the pen, the bed, the door, the basin and the sandal; al-nashīsh: the sound of the boiling of the pot and of a drink; al-ranīn: the sound of the bereaved woman and of the bow; al-qaṣīf: the sound of thunder and the sea, and the roaring of the stallion; al-naqīq: the sound of hens and the frog; al-qaʿqaʿa: the sound of weapons, dry leather and paper; al-gharghara: the sound of the boiling of the pot and the rattling of breath in the chest of the dying; al-ʿajīj: the sound of thunder, women and sheep; al-zafīr: the sound of fire, of the donkey, and of the distressed man when his chest is filled with grief and he breathes it out; al-khashkhasha and al-shakhshakha: the sound of the movement of paper, a new garment and a coat of mail; al-jaljala: the sound of the beast of prey, of thunder and of the movement of bells; al-ḥafīf: the sound of the movement of branches, of a bird's wing and of the movement of a snake; al-ṣalīl and al-ṣalṣala: the sound of iron, the bridle, the sword, dirhams and nails; al-ṭanīn: the sound of the mosquito, the fly and the ṭunbūr (lute); al-aṭīṭ: the sound of the she-camel, the camel-litter, and the man when what is on him weighs him down; al-ṣarṣara: the sound of the falcon and the duck; al-dawiyy: the sound of bees, the ear, rain and thunder; al-inqāḍ: the sound of the hen and the chick; al-taghrīd: the sound of the singer, the camel-driver and the bird — and every one whose voice is melodious is gharid; al-zamzama and al-zahzama: the sound of thunder and the flame of fire, and the imitation of the sound of the Magian when he forces himself to speak with his mouth closed.
